DENT 221.description: Introduction to Dentistry.  History and current role of dental science in the health services field; review of research; overview of dental procedures with laboratory experience and practice observation.

DENT 695.description: Clinic Completion. Course is provided only for the purpose of demonstrating skills in the clinic. It is not available for subject, unit or degree credit. The course may be registered for only as an audit.

DES 102.description: Design Fundamentals. Introduction to the basic elements and processes of visual communication and design. Instruction includes studio projects, lectures and readings. Various media used.

DES 123.description: The Design Challenge: Exploring the Design Process. An overview of the creative design process and introduction to techniques to solve visual problems.

DES 202.description: Design II. Exploration of essential elements of traditional and digital design, including color and image-text integration, editing information, typography and sequencing.

DES 203.description: Digital Design Fundamentals. Exploration of digital processes for the creation of art and design. Centered around the use of the computer and its peripherals for production of 2D media.

DES 213.description: Digital 3D Design. Exploration of digital methods and computational tools for art and design. With an emphasis on three-dimensional physical and virtual output.

DES 230.description: 3D Design: Materials and Tools. Introduction to the study of 3-D Design. Includes a wide investigation of materials, tools, and techniques specific to dimensional design as they apply to package, product, and environmental design.

DES 302.description: Design III. Advanced exploration of typography and image-text integration, including collaborative projects, pre-press and proofing techniques, narrative concepts and information architecture.

DES 303.description: Advanced Digital Design. Exploration of digital processes for art and design with a focus on interactivity, motion, and sound in the virtual realm.

DES 313.description: Graphic Design in Fashion. An intensive studio and lecture course focusing on the applications of graphic design in fashion and related fields.

DES 322.description: Publication Design. Application of layout, typography, design principles and image making in the design and production of books, magazines, zines and digital books.

DES 323.description: Design Theory. A comprehensive study of visual communication focusing on graphic design from 1900 to the present. An introduction to design thinking, language and principles including political and cultural implications.

DES 332A.description: Typography. The study of visual communication through the use of letterforms from historical tradition to contemporary experimental rebellion.

DES 402.description: Advanced Design Projects. Advanced information design within a flexible curriculum. Emphasis on team-oriented projects.

DES 413.description: Professional Practice in Design. A summation of one's practice, with a focus on transitioning to a career as a professional designer.

DES 418.description: Independent Studies in Design. Independent research of specific topics under the direction of a faculty member. Administrative and faculty approval required.

DES 432.description: Special Projects in Design. Students work on projects for outside clients, and receive instruction in professional practices, advanced design techniques, and sophisticated technology. By invitation or portfolio review only. Only open to upper division students.

DES 494A.description: Senior Thesis. Research and writing of a senior-level thesis or thesis project under the supervision of a faculty committee.

DES 494B.description: Senior Thesis. Research and writing of a senior-level thesis or thesis project under the supervision of a faculty committee.

DES 503.description: Contemporary Issues in Design. An analytic seminar of topics, ideas and concepts in the contemporary design world.

DES 514.description: Designers in Residence Forum. Seminar in the professional practice of design featuring formal presentations and mentoring opportunities by designers in residence.

DES 520.description: Individual Studies. Investigation of creative problems through various design media.

DES 530.description: Design Studio Co-Lab. A critical examination of contextual issues, theories, movements and ideas that are relevant to the contemporary design practice in collaboration with a professional client.

DES 535.description: Group Critique. Investigation of issues relative to the student's work in individual studies and thesis; analysis, conceptual development and subjective observations by faculty and student peers.

DES 540.description: Design Pedagogy. A critical examination and application of the issues, theories, and ideas that support the studio practice and teaching of contemporary design.

DES 590.description: Directed Research. Research leading to the master's degree. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department.

DES 591.description: Field Internship Experience. Supervised internship in a design firm, or with an independent designer, on projects and research specific to design practice.

DES 594A.description: Master's Thesis. Credit on acceptance of thesis.

DES 594B.description: Master's Thesis. Credit on acceptance of thesis.

DES 594Z.description: Master's thesis. Credit upon acceptance of master's thesis.

DSR 516.description: Cell and Gene Therapy Development - From Research to Clinic. Introduces the basic principles processes, and requirements of cell and gene therapy drug development, manufacturing and clinical applications using hands-on and interactive activities.

DSR 574.description: Stem Cell and Developmental Biology Seminar Series. Selected topics in Development, Stem Cell, and Regeneration.

DSR 626.description: Bioinformatic Methods: Transcriptome and Chromatin Analysis. Principles of bioinformatic and computational analysis methods applicable to genomic, epigenomic and molecular biology studies.

DSR 790.description: Research. Research leading to the doctorate. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Open only to doctoral students. Graded CR/NC.

DSR 794A.description: Doctoral Dissertation. Credit on acceptance of dissertation. Graded IP/CR/NC. Open only to doctoral students.

DSR 794B.description: Doctoral Dissertation. Credit on acceptance of dissertation. Graded IP/CR/NC. Open only to doctoral students.

DSR 794C.description: Doctoral Dissertation. Credit on acceptance of dissertation. Graded IP/CR/NC. Open only to doctoral students.

DSR 794D.description: Doctoral Dissertation. Credit on acceptance of dissertation. Graded IP/CR/NC. Open only to doctoral students.

DSR 794Z.description: Doctoral Dissertation. Credit on acceptance of dissertation. Graded IP/CR/NC. Open only to doctoral students.

DMM 500.description: Principles and Theories of Digital Media Management. Explores the digital media environment, its sociohistorical evolution and the impact of digital technologies and media on practices within cultural and business ecosystems.

DMM 505.description: Digital Audience Research and Analysis. Explores research methodologies and digital audience analytics, evaluating online audience needs and wants and focusing on data-driven and ethical decision making.

DMM 510.description: Digital Media Buying, Measurement and Analytics. Examines digital media advertising sales technologies: digital advertising, media buying, digital asset performance measurement and data collection methodologies used for business planning.

DMM 515.description: Digital Content, Production and Distribution. Explores the evolution of digital media content, content categories in digital media, innovations in content production techniques and technologies and the digital distribution revolution.

DMM 520.description: Strategic Digital Media Marketing. Case studies and examples to ideate, create and evaluate cutting-edge techniques used to implement long-range strategies for ethical digital media management and marketing.

DMM 525.description: Digital Media Leadership. Examines personal leadership principles and practices applicable to digital media, focused on leading within organizations, building diverse, high-performing teams and delivering digital media initiatives.

DMM 530.description: Managing Digital Media Teams and Projects. Covers the principles and skills needed to manage teams and projects within the digital media environment and achieve organizational goals through strategic planning.

DMM 535.description: Digital Content Direction. Covers principles and strategies for directing digital content across platforms to achieve organizational objectives beyond creating awareness, informing or entertaining.

DMM 540.description: Developing Effective User Engagement Strategies. Covers strategies to balance the needs of creating a user experience and content with the ethical imperatives of fostering equity, diversity and inclusion.

DMM 545.description: Digital Platforms: Disruptions and Directions. Explores how the platform economy is disrupting traditional marketplaces and industries with new, digital technologies and ways for optimizing outcomes from those changes.

DMM 550.description: Digital Media Innovation and Entrepreneurship. Covers management of digital media innovation within digital media organizations and new entrepreneurial ventures, and ways for alleviating challenges to equity and diversity.

DMM 555.description: Digital Media Management Capstone. Students create an innovative idea or initiative that solves a problem or achieves a goal within a digital media organization or business unit.

DSM 520.description: Managing Technologies for Digital Media. Strategies and decision-making for development and management of online sites, mobile apps and social platforms, including search optimization, monetization, product development and user experience testing.

DSM 521.description: Streaming Entertainment: Innovation and Impact. Explores the cultural, technological and economic forces behind media-streaming platforms, with industry leaders sharing insights, and students creating their own channels.

DSM 526.description: Digital Media Product Management. Digital media product management using case studies and real-world projects. Customer discovery, strategy, roadmaps and product requirements.

DSM 529.description: The Future of Advertising: AdTech Innovations and AI Trends. Programmatic advertising, adtech and AI trends through hands-on digital marketing projects with real clients, media dollars, ad platforms and student team-led client partnership.

DSM 530.description: Brand Strategy for Digital Media. Exploration of the essential art of branding in the digital age; building relationships between consumers and brands

DSM 531.description: Podcasting for Brand Building. Explores the role of podcasts in brand development. Students learn production, positioning, promotion, analytics and monetization while creating their own podcasts.

DSM 559.description: Social Media for Social Impact. Explores how social media campaigns can address such global issues as climate change and inequality, with an emphasis on ethics, transparency and analytics.

DSM 591.description: Digital Social Media Internship. Integration of practical experiences with academic learning to apply digital media strategies, design and innovation in creating impactful solutions, fostering critical thinking and problem-solving skills.

DSM 596.description: Final Project Capstone. Students produce a working site, app or embedded social platform project with digital/multimedia elements. Development includes pitching, conceptualization and launching of the final project.

DSM 599.description: Special Topics. Special Topics in Digital Social Media.

SCDC 435.description: How Washington Really Works. Provides students with a DC insider's understanding of American politics, campaigning and elections.

THTR 101.description: Introduction to Acting. Study of diverse genres and disciplines of acting; fundamental techniques necessary for performance; scene study from contemporary text.

THTR 105.description: Introduction to Screen Acting. Introduction to the theoretical and foundational practices, techniques and strategies specific to screen acting in relation to the basic dynamics of acting for the stage.

THTR 120B.description: Acting I. Basic principles and techniques of acting through theatre games and improvisation. Introduction to contemporary texts, basic characterization and cold reading techniques.

THTR 122.description: Improvisation and Theatre Games. Individual and group exercises to free the actor physically and emotionally and to stimulate creativity, imagination, and  self-expression.

THTR 130.description: Introduction to Theatrical Production. Introduction to the non-performance areas of theatrical production(administrative, design, and technical fields) through hands-onparticipation in USC productions.

THTR 131B.description: Advanced Theatrical Production. Advanced understanding of non-performance areas of theatrical production (administrative, design, and technical fields) through hands-on participation in USC productions.

THTR 132B.description: Art of Theatrical Design. Development of the artistic process and theatrical design vocabulary of the individual within the environment of collaborative storytelling.

THTR 141.description: Beginning Voice. Physiological mechanism of voice: breath control, phonation, resonance, articulation of language for the stage; expressive use of stress, intonation and rhythm.

THTR 152.description: Introduction to Scene Study: Contemporary Plays. Application and consolidation of the skills, knowledge and techniques acquired in the study of fundamentals of acting encountered in THTR 101.

THTR 192.description: History of Stand-Up Comedy. A comprehensive overview and understanding of how stand-up evolved in the United States, from the mid-1800's to the current touring performers.

THTR 197.description: Comedy and Performance. Comedy and Performance traces the history of comedy in performance from its earliest incarnations to the present day.

THTR 202.description: The Fundamentals of Comedy. Introduction to the fundamental elements of comedy and how to apply those elements to create short, original pieces of comedy in performance and writing.

THTR 205.description: Stardom: Creation, Management and Culture Impact. An exploration of the phenomena of stardom and celebrity across media, entertainment, sports and social influence, ranging from early modern theatre to current day.

THTR 213.description: Corset Construction. Design and construct period corsets, along with the materials and terminology needed to sew (machine and hand) corsets.

THTR 214B.description: The Actor's Instrument: Voice and Body. A comprehensive exploration of voice, speech and acting to strengthen the actors physical instrument.

THTR 216.description: Movement for Actors. Training and practice in the coordination of the physical          apparatus of the actor utilizing various movement techniques       through improvisation.

THTR 220B.description: Intermediate Acting I. Continuing development of imagination leading to an increased range of dramatic expression through the formalized text of William Shakespeare.

THTR 225.description: Theatre Across History and Cultures. The analysis of a range of plays from different times and cultures with a consideration of the roles of actor, director, dramaturg and designer.

THTR 229.description: Sports on Stage and Screen. The examination of the intersection between athletes and actors through the study of plays, musicals, feature films and TV series that depict athletic worlds.

THTR 230.description: Theatrical Design as Poetic Realism. The visualization and communication of design ideas through free-hand and mechanical drawing, as well as advanced dramaturgical storytelling and the creative collaborative process.

THTR 232.description: Introduction to Theatrical Lighting. Theory and practice of theatrical lighting design including electricity, radiant energy, refraction, reflection, absorption, chromatic variation and electronic controls.

THTR 241.description: Methods and Materials. Cutting-edge and traditional methods and materials that enhance both the planning stages and realization of the theatrical design.

THTR 250.description: Camera and Improvisation. Understanding on-camera acting and improvisation by creating original material both in front and behind the camera.

THTR 252A.description: Intermediate Acting I: Drama/Comedy. Polishing the actor's skills through analysis and performance applied to the arc of a character.  The 'a' section of the course will cover drama and the 'b' section will focus on comedy.

THTR 252B.description: Intermediate Acting I: Drama/Comedy. Polishing the actor's skills through analysis and performance applied to the arc of a character.  The 'a' section of the course will cover drama and the 'b' section will focus on comedy.

THTR 295.description: Theatre in Los Angeles. Current state of American theatre, through a study of acting, playwriting, criticism, stage design, lighting, and dramatic styles.

THTR 302.description: Shakespeare in His World. The plays and theatre of Shakespeare, the influences on his work  and his contemporary world. Recommended preparation: THTR 201,  THTR 310, THTR 311

THTR 303.description: Projection Design I. Investigation of the projection design process, equipment, multi-media, digital technology concepts and related documentation.

THTR 305A.description: Directing. Examination of basic directorial principles. Pre-production analysis and rehearsal procedures; relationship of the director to actor; integration of technical aspects of production.

THTR 305B.description: Directing.  Examination of basic directorial principles. Pre-production analysis and rehearsal procedures; relationship of the director to actor; integration of technical aspects of production.

THTR 306.description: Audio-Drama. Develop a basic understanding of the skills required to effectively develop, create, record, edit and market an audio drama.

THTR 308.description: Lighting Programming for Live Events. Strategies and principles in computerized programming for theatrical lighting, emphasizing its applied use in creating kinetic, responsive environments.

THTR 315B.description: Physical Theatre I. Actor training anchored by rigorous physical movements.   Activities include comedy, clowning, juggling, and mask work.   Open to BFA acting majors only.

THTR 316.description: Advanced Movement for Actors. Advanced physical training and practice for the BA actor utilizing various movement techniques through improvisation.

THTR 317.description: Theatre Clown. Introduction to techniques of clown performance and key techniques including complicite, play, looks and drops.

THTR 318.description: Creating the Hit Podcast. Develops the ability to create a podcast. Focuses on skills to produce, perform, market and monetize a podcast across a variety of genres.

THTR 320B.description: Intermediate Acting II. Further development of range and breadth of performance skills with emphasis on texts of heightened language and style.

THTR 322.description: Improv 2: Advanced Improv. An in depth study of improvised comedy scene work.  An exploration of the primary tools and structure for creating improvised scenes and developing characters for stage and screen.

THTR 325.description: Casting for Stage and Screen. Introduction of the casting principles and practices for four of the mediums that dominate entertainment: theatre, film, television and commercials.

THTR 335.description: Scenic Construction. Technology, organization, and operation of the theatrical scene shop centered around the proper and safe use of tools, the choosing of materials, and methods of construction.

THTR 336.description: Sound Design I. The art and techniques of theatrical sound design. The use of music and ambient sound in theatrical presentations. Design elements as metaphor.

THTR 339B.description: The Actor's Instrument: Voice and Body II. Continued training in the areas of breath awareness, physical awareness, voice, speech work and movement training.

THTR 342A.description: Basic Voice.  a: Examination of the individual voice centering on resonance, tone, flexibility, and support through dramatic selections for transmitting meaning and emotion of character.

THTR 342B.description: Basic Voice. Examination of the individual voice centering on resonance, tone, flexibility, and support through dramatic selections for transmitting meaning and emotion of character. Continuation of 342a.

THTR 343.description: Musical Theatre Audition. Designed to give students confidence and integrity for auditions in musical theatre. Choosing appropriate material and preparation for the audition and performance. Audition required.

THTR 345.description: Acting for Global Cinema. Explore global acting techniques, cultural sensitivity and international traditions, preparing students to authentically portray diverse characters.

THTR 346.description: Musical Theatre Sound Reinforcement. A hands-on course in the use of microphones and music theory skills to reinforce all instrument sections in a typical musical theatre pit.

THTR 349.description: Costume Crafts: Armor and Millinery. An overview of costume crafts construction techniques as they relate to the more structured of crafts. Hat, jewelry, shoe and armor construction techniques are explored.

THTR 352B.description: Intermediate Acting II. Building and sustaining character with special focus on stylized realism, subtext and heightened language. Multi-cultural text and methodologies.

THTR 354.description: Acting Shakespeare. Basic approach to the acting and analysis of the highly formalized texts of William Shakespeare.

THTR 355.description: Acting for Sitcoms. Provide an understanding as to how to work in half-hour television and streaming media.

THTR 365.description: Playwriting I.  Essential elements of playwriting through weekly assignments, students' initiative, occasional productions of scenes, and extensive classroom analysis.

THTR 366.description: Playwriting II.  Continuation of the work begun in 365.

THTR 395.description: Drama as Human Relations. A focus on American ethnic and multicultural diversity from the  perspectives of gender, race, and myth as revealed in plays, film,  and other performance media.

THTR 397.description: Theatre Practicum. Substantive participation in a production sponsored by the School and supervised by the faculty.

THTR 401.description: Contemporary Theatre in a Changing World. Explores the bold approaches that characterize the best of contemporary theatre, as well as the artists who are groundbreakers in a changing world.

THTR 404.description: Acting Theory. Examination of the theoretical foundations of acting as an art form through the reading of primary historical texts.

THTR 405.description: Performing Identities. This course explores the live performance medium as a creative means of social redress and personal expression. Duplicates credit in the former THTR 393m.

THTR 406.description: Theatre on the Edge. An exploration of the art of theatre at the edge of possibilities.

THTR 407B.description: Drawing and Rendering for the Theater. Drawing and rendering techniques appropriate for theater designers. Drawing and drawing theory.

THTR 408A.description: Dialects. The study of standard American stage dialect using the international phonetic alphabet.

THTR 408B.description: Dialects. The study of accents and regional dialects.

THTR 409.description: Advanced Drafting: Vectorworks. An exploration of computer aided drafting (CAD) software, including drafting standards as achieved with Vectorworks and related software.

THTR 410.description: The Digital Actor. Empowers the student to forge a career in acting by managing and utilizing the many facets of social and digital media.

THTR 411.description: The Business of Acting. Develops the student's ability to connect and combine managerial, economic and business-related skills with the craft and career of acting.

THTR 417.description: Stage Combat. Introduction to safe and effective portrayals of violence for the stage. Training and practice of unarmed stage combat skills. Recommended preparation: THTR 216.

THTR 419.description: Alexander Technique for Performers. Training and practice in the work of F.M. Alexander. A clear and systematic look into the underlying principles that govern human movement.

THTR 421.description: Public Speaking as Performance: A Course for Non-Actors. Public speaking approached as performance, using acting techniques to communicate with confidence, clarity and charisma.

THTR 422.description: Improv 3 : Long Form Improvisation. Emphasis on  Full Length Improvised Performances including the  styles of various playwrights, genres of films, "the Harold,  "improvised plays and musicals. Building on the groundwork of THTR  122 Improvisation and Theatre Games and THTR 322 Improv 2,  students apply the techniques to long form unscripted performances.

THTR 423.description: Magic. The dramatic art of making an audience believe something is impossible. the history and performance of magic including illusion, mentalism, vanishing, coin and card tricks.

THTR 424.description: Creator as Entrepreneur. Explores the tools required to forge a career as a contemporary creator, with an emphasis on producing and monetizing new work through modern platforms.

THTR 425.description: Dynamics of Technical Theatre. Advanced technical direction topics involving the technical analysis and design of moving scenery and theatrical systems.

THTR 427.description: Audition Technique for Film, Television and New Media. Develop on-camera auditioning skills for actors at a professional level in a variety of film, television and new media venues.

THTR 430.description: Stage Management II. Application of stage management procedures required in the professional theatre.

THTR 431.description: Seminar in Theatre Design. Research into the application of contemporary topics relevant to theatrical design within the diverse cultural environment of the greater Los Angeles area.

THTR 432B.description: Scene Design II.  Continuation of THTR 330. Evolution of scene design through  analysis of script, environmental factors, and styles.

THTR 433B.description: Costume Design II: The Psychology of Fashion. Evolution of costume design through analysis of script, environmental factors, and styles.

THTR 434B.description: Lighting Design II.  Continuation of THTR 332. Evolution of lighting design through    analysis of script, environmental factors, and styles.

THTR 435.description: Advanced Theatrical Drafting: AutoCAD. Drafting style and complex graphic communication. Emphasis on creating professional plates, developing an individual style and graphic problem solving.

THTR 437.description: Scene Painting. Techniques, materials, and equipment of the scenic artist  including both historic and modern methods. Recommended  preparation: paint and drawing experience

THTR 438.description: Technical Theatre. Theory and practice of technical theatre. Emphasis is on technical problem solving and graphic solutions to technical theatre.

THTR 441.description: Digital Sound Mixing. Advanced exploration of theatrical sound design theory and related technology; creative uses of music, sound effects, and audio equipment in modern theatres.

THTR 442.description: Voice-over Acting. Acting techniques, recording studio technology and editing for the field of voice acting and voice-overs.

THTR 445.description: Developing Your Speaking Voice. Development of resonance, range and clarity. Examination of posture and breathwork.  Applications of voice skills to acting, professional speaking and personal projects.

THTR 447.description: Fashion Influencing. Analysis of key influencers and aesthetics within relevant digital platforms for the fashion industry.

THTR 448.description: History of Fashion and the Costume: A Guide to Glamour. Introduction to four hundred years of fashion history drawing parallels between the fashion and period that it existed.

THTR 453.description: Taking it on the Road and Beyond. Specific instruction to prepare Stage Managers for the rigors and processes of Touring and Opera productions as well as other non-theatrical team-based collaborations in entertainment.

THTR 454.description: Acting Shakespeare II. A continuation and deeper investigation of the analysis and performance of the highly formalized texts of William Shakespeare.

THTR 456.description: Latinx Theatre. Explores the range and genealogy of Latinx theatre and performance from its origins in the last fifty years to the present.

THTR 457.description: Film Acting Practicum. Creating a visual narrative story. Gaining a basic understanding of both the visual and technical components of story telling.

THTR 460.description: Asian and Asian American Theatre: Identity and Aesthetics. Explores Asian and Asian American theatre, from the historical to  the contemporary, with an aim toward understanding issues of  aesthetics, acculturation, and identity.

THTR 464.description: An Actor's Reel. Using original and existing scripted material for film, television and new media students will act, film and edit scenes to form a professional performance reel.

THTR 465.description: Playwriting III.  Analysis of a full-length play or its equivalent with continued production opportunity.

THTR 467.description: Going Viral: Performance for New Media. A writing and performance course (partially online) for new media. Students will learn to create original short form and web series content for new media including YouTube, Funny or Die, Periscope and other Internet platforms.

THTR 471.description: Industry Landscape. Designed to provide the graduating students with opportunity to select, prepare and perform for agents, directors and producers in film, television and theatre. Also includes the study of the business of acting.

THTR 473.description: Sketch Comedy in Performance. A workshop in the techniques of performing humorous sketches, in collaboration with writers, directors, and technicians in the production of a live sketch comedy show. Recommended preparation: THTR 101, THTR 122, THTR 470.

THTR 474.description: Introduction to Stand Up Comedy. An introduction to the discipline of conceiving, writing, and creating original Stand Up Comedy routines

THTR 475.description: Acting on Camera: The Collaborative Process. Acting students will learn to develop on-camera acting skills and to collaborate with student directors and cinematographers from the School of Cinematic Arts.

THTR 476.description: African American Theatre, Dance, and Performance. A survey of African American theatre and cultural performance traditions as a reflection of both African American culture and American history.

THTR 479.description: Solo Performance. A writing-performance workshop in which students write, develop,  and rehearse original, autobiographical and character monologues  and perform them at the end of the semester.

THTR 480A.description: Performance for Camera. Structured to address the dynamics of acting in relation to film/television. Refining the students' understanding of the similarities/differences between acting on stage/film.

THTR 480B.description: Performance for Camera. Continued exploration of acting for film/television. Furthering the student's understanding of the similarities/differences between acting on stage/film.

THTR 482.description: Stand Up 2: Becoming A Pro. Interactive performance and writing intensive focusing on creating professional level comedy material plus onstage performance strategies.

THTR 484.description: Acting in Television Commercials. An on-camera, workshop-style introduction to techniques, perspectives and theories unique to performing in television commercials.

THTR 488.description: Theatre in the Community. Research and actively develop the theory of theatre as a movingpolitical, social, economic and spiritual force of change withinthe local community.

THTR 489.description: Theatre Internship. Practical experience in the entertainment industry.

THTR 490.description: Directed Research.  Individual research and readings. Not available for graduate credit.

THTR 493B.description: Periods and Styles.  A survey of the influence of historical and cultural events on the evaluation of theatrical styles. Restoration to 20th century.

THTR 495.description: Experimental Theatre Workshop I. Guidance and direction in the production of new and experimental plays for a public audience. By audition.

THTR 497.description: Advanced Theatre Practicum. Intensive participation in a production sponsored by the school and supervised by the faculty, to increase and develop artistic growth.

THTR 501.description: Poetry and Prose into Drama. Plays for the stage shall be written using public-domain poetry and prose as inspiration and source material, complemented with exploring poetry, prose, and varied dramas as context for the student writer. Students should be well-versed in literature, and have written in one or more genres.

THTR 515B.description: Advanced Movement. Advanced exercises in movement for the use of the body in relation to the stage.

THTR 515D.description: Advanced Movement. Advanced exercises in movement for the use of the body in relation to the stage including a study of Viewpoints and Mask Work.

THTR 516.description: Filmmaking for Actors. The execution and breakdown of a film project from ideation to completion.

THTR 520B.description: Advanced Acting. Advanced training in acting skills including camera work; emphasis upon individual needs.

THTR 520D.description: Advanced Acting.  Advanced training in acting skills; emphasis upon individual needs.

THTR 520E.description: Advanced Acting. Advanced training in acting skills; includes performing for agents, directors and producers in film, television and theatre.

THTR 529B.description: Textual Studies for Performance. Close textual reading of dramatic texts as a fundamental tool for  rehearsal and performance.

THTR 540B.description: Advanced Voice Diction.  Individual work in improving the actor's vocal range.

THTR 540D.description: Advanced Voice Diction.  Individual work in improving the actor's vocal range.

THTR 540F.description: Advanced Voice Diction. Advanced individual vocal development and application to a variety of professional and performance circumstances including voice-over work.

THTR 566.description: Dramatic Writing Studio. Investigates gestalt of the student dramatic writer's professional development from the empty page and writing fundamentals to the first-draft script, business affairs, and dramaturgical advancement.

THTR 571.description: Professional Seminar. Introduction to the world of the professional actor.

THTR 580B.description: Performance with Camera. Structured to address the dynamics of acting in relation to film/television. Refining the students understanding of the similarities/differences between acting on stage/film.

THTR 582B.description: Dramatic Narrative Design. Continued exploration of the execution and breakdown of a film project, including script development and production techniques, through hands-on collaboration.

THTR 590.description: Directed Research.  Research leading to the Master's Degree. Maximum units which may  be applied to the degree to be determined by the department.   Graded CR/NC.

THTR 596.description: Thesis Development and Attainment. Designed to guide the MFADW student toward refinement of thesis including vision, development, and execution.

THTR 597.description: Theatre Practicum. Substantive participation in productions sponsored by the school and supervised by the faculty.

THTE 107.description: Foundations of Vocal Performance. Exploration of the foundations of vocal technique in a group setting, with an emphasis on musical theatre repertoire.

THTE 201A.description: Acting for Musical Theatre. Analysis and investigation of role interpretation and character development by working on two or more scenes from the same play. Introduction of techniques to unlock objectives based on the text.

THTE 201B.description: Acting for Musical Theatre. Continuation of analysis and investigation of role interpretation and character development by working on two or more scenes from the same play. Introduction of techniques to unlock objectives for character creation.

THTE 203.description: Speech. A guided study of dialect acquisition.

THTE 206B.description: Movement for Musical Theatre. Introduction to foundational skills for musical theatre movement, including safe alignment and a movement vocabulary.

THTE 208.description: Musicianship for Musical Theatre Actors II. Continued development of the foundations of musicianship necessary for a career in musical theatre.

THTE 226.description: The History of Content Creation. An exploration of the evolution of content creation spanning from the ancient multicultural oral traditions to the digital age.  Discover how storytellers and story-sellers have always been influencers in the realms of entertainment, activism and commerce.

THTE 300.description: Script and Score. Introduction and development of techniques needed to transition from the script to score. Beginning with an exploration of Broadway's "Golden Age" and the examination of Sondheim and his contemporaries.

THTE 340.description: Musical Theatre Integration Workshop I. Introduction to the synthesis of emotional life, voice and movement skills as the foundation for an authentic musical theatre performance.

THTE 350B.description: Musical Theatre Integration Workshop II. Continuation of the techniques developed in THTE 350aL to heighten dramatic text for musical theatre.

THTE 354.description: Musical Theatre Individual Instruction. Introduction to foundational healthy vocal performance/singing skills needed to sustain a career in the musical theatre.

THTE 407.description: Building Your Cabaret. Development of skills needed to create a solo musical cabaret performance.

THTE 450B.description: Musical Theatre Integration Workshop III. The investigation of various musical theatre roles in preparation for entering the entertainment industry.

EALC 101.description: Conversational Chinese and Intercultural Communication. Basic Mandarin conversational skills for effective communication in familiar, everyday Chinese contexts and better understanding of intercultural communication through content-based language acquisition. Graded CR/NC. Not available for credit to East Asian Area Studies, East Asian Languages and Cultures, and East Asian Studies majors and minors.

EALC 102.description: Language, Art and Culture: Calligraphy. This course introduces students to the origin of the basic  components of Chinese scripts and the basic principles and styles  of calligraphy.

EALC 104.description: Chinese I. The sound system of modern Chinese; aural comprehension, oral expression, basic patterns, and writing system.

EALC 106.description: Chinese II. Dialogue practice and conversation; reading of simple stories and essays; comparison of Chinese and English grammar; writing of paragraphs.

EALC 109.description: Extensive Reading in Chinese. Develops reading fluency in Chinese through the Extensive Reading method, emphasizing large-volume reading with minimal unfamiliar vocabulary to build comprehension and enjoyment.

EALC 115.description: Korean I. Basic Korean conversation practice, aural comprehension, basic grammar and building proficiency of reading and writing with Hangul (Korean alphabet).

EALC 117.description: Korean II. Continuation of EALC 115, basic conversation practice, aural comprehension, basic grammar and building proficiency of reading and writing.

EALC 120.description: Japanese I. Basic Japanese conversation practice, basic grammar and building proficiency of reading and writing Hiragana and Katakana (Japanese alphabetical systems) and some basic kanji (Chinese characters).

EALC 121.description: Extensive Reading in Japanese I. Development of reading skill in Japanese for elementary level students through short stories written for learners of Japanese and authentic materials written for native Japanese speakers.

EALC 122.description: Japanese II. Continuation of EALC 120.  Basic Japanese conversation practice,  basic grammar and building proficiency of reading and writing  Hiragana and Katakana and basic kanji.

EALC 125.description: Introduction to Contemporary East Asian Cinema and Culture. An introduction to and overview of the contemporary cinemas of East Asia: China (Hong Kong, the People's Republic, and Taiwan), Japan, and Korea.

EALC 130.description: Introduction to East Asian Ethical Thought. Foundations of East Asian ethical and philosophical thought and how they apply to modern ethical issues, such as the death penalty, abortion or climate change.

EALC 204.description: Chinese III. Conversational practice: reading of stories and essays; writing of short essays.

EALC 206.description: Chinese IV. Continuation of 204, with emphasis on reading and writing, frequent interaction with native speakers.

EALC 215.description: Korean III.  Drill to increase proficiency in dialogue, reading, and writing;  intermediate level readings.

EALC 217.description: Korean IV.  Advanced level reading of modern Korean and exercises in written  composition.

EALC 220.description: Japanese III. Continuation of EALC 122.  Conversation practice, basic to  intermediate grammar, and building proficiency of reading and  writing Hiragana and Katakana with additional kanji.

EALC 221.description: Extensive Reading in Japanese II. Development of reading skills in Japanese for intermediate level students through short stories written for learners of Japanese and authentic materials written for native speakers.

EALC 222.description: Japanese IV. Continuation of EALC 220. More sophisticated grammar and  vocabulary for natural conversation. Enhancing fundamental reading  and writing skills, expanding the knowledge of kanji.

EALC 250.description: Nation, Culture and Power in East Asia. Analyzes political power, nationalism and cultural identity in East Asia. Topics addressed include multiculturalism, migration and ethnic politics, in addition to theories of nationalism.

EALC 304.description: Advanced Modern Chinese I.  Reading selections from different styles of modern Chinese        writings, analysis of stylistic techniques and syntactic           structure, composition, and translation.

EALC 306.description: Advanced Modern Chinese II.  Continuation of 304; composition exercises in different styles of writing.

EALC 317.description: Advanced Korean II. Continuation of EALC 315, with emphasis on the use of Chinese  characters, translation, and composition exercises.

EALC 320.description: Advanced Japanese I. Strengthen intermediate Japanese language proficiency.  Oral/aural  communication skills as well as reading and writing skills.   Promote an understanding of the present-day Japanese culture.

EALC 322.description: Advanced Japanese II. Continuation of EALC 320.  Improve and strengthen abilities to  speak, listen, read and write, coping with more involved materials  and situation.

EALC 331.description: Encountering Japanese Religions. The development of religious thought and practice in the Japanese islands, with Buddhism and Shinto being the most prominent.

EALC 333.description: Introduction to Korean Film. Survey of Korean film, the film industry and critical issues from the colonial period to the present.

EALC 358.description: Transnational Chinese Literature and Culture. An introduction to Sinophone literatures and cultures (in English translation) from the Asia-Pacific region, including Taiwan, Hong Kong, Tibet, Southeast Asia, and North America.

EALC 366.description: Chinese Professional Internship: Communication and Culture. Combined classroom discussion and supervised internship at companies. Practical experience in applying communication and cultural knowledge in a professional, "real world" employment context.

EALC 407.description: News and Web Chinese. Reading selections from newspaper articles and online reports to further develop proficiency in advanced Chinese and understanding of the society and culture.

EALC 420.description: Advanced Oral Communication in Japanese. Development of advanced oral communication skills in Japanese, fostering cultural understanding and practical communication for diverse academic, professional, and social contexts.

EALC 432.description: Premodern Korean Literature and Storytelling. Development of Korean literature from ancient times to the nineteenth century, including major canonical works. Conducted in English.

EALC 455.description: Japanese Fiction.  Japanese fiction from early to modern times; literary, philosophical, and social aspects of tales and novels. Conducted in English.

EALC 465.description: Topics in Korean Visual and Cultural Studies. Examination of dominant and emergent critical issues in the study of modern and contemporary Korean visual culture.

EALC 490.description: Directed Research.  Individual research and readings. Not available for graduate credit.

EALC 494A.description: Honors Thesis. Research and writing of original thesis under guidance of faculty  member.

EALC 494B.description: Honors Thesis. Research and writing of original thesis under guidance of faculty  member.

EALC 506.description: Selections from Classical Chinese Literature. Examination of recent scholarship on classical Chinese literature alongside readings from major genres of Chinese literary history. English translations provided.

EALC 510.description: Contemporary Japanese Cinema. Japanese cinema since the 1980s focusing on the works by filmmakers.

EALC 588A.description: Directed Readings.  Assigned readings according to individual needs.

EALC 588B.description: Directed Readings.  Assigned readings according to individual needs.

EALC 590.description: Directed Research.  Research leading tothe Master's Degree. Maximum units which may be applied tothe degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

EALC 594A.description: Master's Thesis. Credit on acceptance of Thesis. Graded CR/NC.

EALC 594B.description: Master's Thesis. Credit on acceptance of Thesis. Graded CR/NC.

EALC 594Z.description: Master's Thesis. Credit on acceptance of Thesis. Graded CR/NC.

EALC 650.description: Research Seminar in Chinese Documents. An introduction to the different genres of documents for the study of Chinese civilization, and training in their use.

EALC 700.description: Professionalization Seminar for Advanced Graduate Students. Familiarizes advanced graduate students with topics relevant to academic work in East Asian humanities, including research planning, dissertation writing, publishing, and conference presentation.

EALC 794A.description: Doctoral Dissertation. Credit on acceptance of dissertation. Graded IP/CR/NC.

EALC 794B.description: Doctoral Dissertation. Credit on acceptance of dissertation. Graded IP/CR/NC.

EALC 794C.description: Doctoral Dissertation. Credit on acceptance of dissertation. Graded IP/CR/NC.

EALC 794D.description: Doctoral Dissertation. Credit on acceptance of dissertation. Graded IP/CR/NC.

EALC 794Z.description: Doctoral Dissertation. Credit on acceptance of dissertation. Graded IP/CR/NC.

EASC 160.description: China and the World. Advanced-level introduction to China and its relations with the wider world in historic and contemporary perspective.

EASC 490.description: Directed Research. Individual research and readings. Not available for graduate credit.

EASC 495.description: Honors Thesis. Writing the honors thesis: for East Asian Area Studies Honors majors.

EASC 590.description: Directed Research. Research leading to the Master's degree. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

EASC 594A.description: Master's Thesis. Credit on acceptance of thesis. Graded IP/CR/NC.

EASC 594B.description: Master's Thesis. Credit on acceptance of thesis. Graded IP/CR/NC.

EASC 594Z.description: Master's Thesis. Credit on acceptance of thesis. Graded IP/CR/NC.

EASC 595.description: Research Methods and Prospectus Writing. Research skills to launch a specific research project, usually a master's thesis.

EASC 596.description: Internship for Curricular Practical Training. Part-time or full-time, practical work experience in the student's field of study. The internship must be located at an off-campus facility. Students are individually supervised by faculty. May not be taken until the student has completed at least one semester of enrollment in the graduate program with a cumulative 3.0 GPA.

ECON 101.description: Free People, Free Thought and Free Markets. The philosophical foundations of modern political and economic thought, including economic rationality, neoclassical economics, free-market vs. socialist economies and behavioral economics.

ECON 203.description: Principles of Microeconomics. Behavior of firms and consumers, functions of the price system, competition and monopoly, labor markets, poverty, government regulation, international trade, and the environment.

ECON 205.description: Principles of Macroeconomics. Unemployment, inflation and output determination and links.Effects of government taxation and spending on growth, investment,saving, consumption, and trade.

ECON 303.description: Intermediate Microeconomic Theory. Decision-making by business firms, consumer preferences and behavior, uncertainty, competition, monopoly, labor and resource markets, efficient resource allocation, externalities, and government policy.

ECON 305.description: Intermediate Macroeconomic Theory. The determinants of aggregate income, employment, and inflation; economic fluctuations; fiscal and monetary policy; financial markets; the national debt.

ECON 317.description: Introduction to Statistics for Economists. Introduction to statistical methods appropriate for analyzing economic data: probability theory, random variables and probability distributions, sampling, estimation, statistical inference.

ECON 318.description: Introduction to Econometrics. Application of statistical methods to economic data: estimating economic relationships using regression analysis, testing hypotheses involving economic behavior, forecasting economic variables.

ECON 333.description: Innovation Economics and Business: Beer, AI and Video Games. Analyze varied industries using legal, business, and economic  principles. Emphasis is on how these forces shape marketing  strategies.

ECON 339.description: Philosophy of Economics. Central topics in the philosophy of economics, including models of economic rationality, the aggregation of preferences and the conditions in which markets yield undesirable outcomes.

ECON 340.description: Economics of Less Developed Countries. Causes of economic underdevelopment: historical, institutional,    structural, ideological, technological, cultural. Patterns and     theories of development. Role of government, international trade,  and education in economic growth.

ECON 346.description: Economics of Transition and Development: China. A focus on the Chinese economy, its reform and transition to a  market economy, its relation with East Asian countries and  integration into the world economy.

ECON 351.description: Microeconomics for Business. Development and business applications of: theory of the firm;      theory of the consumer; inter-temporaldecisions; decisions under   risk; market failures; industrial and enterprise structure.        Prerequisites: MATH 118 or MATH 125 or MATH 126 or MATH 226. Not   for major credit for: Economics, Economics/Mathematics, Social     Sciences (Economics). Duplicates credit in BUAD 351.

ECON 352.description: Macroeconomics for Business. Theoretical development and significance to business and markets   of economic growth; inflation;unemployment; monetary and fiscal    policy; business cycles; savings and investment; exchange rates.   Corequisite: ECON 351. Recommended preparation: introductory       economics course, high school math, and algebra. Not for major     credit for: Economics, Economics/Mathematics, Social Sciences      (Economics). Duplicates credit in BUAD 352.

ECON 357.description: Money, Credit, and Banking. The money, bond, stock, and other financial markets; portfolio     choice; determinants of asset prices and interest rates;           inflation; interactions between financial markets and government   policies.

ECON 361.description: Understanding Financial Crises. Key facts and basic mechanisms concerning financial crises and related topics (bank runs, sovereign default decision, currency collapse).

ECON 379.description: Economic Policy Analysis. Main frameworks, theories, practices of applied economics policy in real-world settings; creating competencies for elected officials, central bank personnel, public administrators, regulators, nonprofit executives, implementers and evaluators.

ECON 395.description: Economic Policy Issues. Selected policy dilemmas in economics. Topics vary.

ECON 405.description: Neuroeconomics. Introduction to the methodology used in experimental neuroeconomics and discussion of neural correlates of decision-making. Prerequisite: ECON 303.

ECON 415.description: Behavioral Economics. Examination of the traditional and behavioral theories of decision-making and the state of the art in the field. Prerequisite: ECON 303.

ECON 438.description: Values and Social Analysis. Factors that make values an essential feature of human society; how values develop, change and are abandoned; role of values in economic development.

ECON 451.description: The Politics of International Trade. Economic approaches and political processes are used to explain observed international trade policy choices. Topics covered include globalization, regionalism, labor standards, the environment and sanctions. Recommended preparation: Micro- and Macroeconomics.

ECON 457.description: Financial Markets. General equilibrium analysis of economics with financial markets; decision making under uncertainty; methods of risk reduction; portfolio theory and valuation of securities; efficiency of security markets.

ECON 460.description: Economic Applications of Machine Learning. A capstone course that introduces state-of-the-art estimation methods for high-dimensional data.

ECON 464.description: The Principles of Market Design. Fundamental principles in designing successful market mechanisms to allocate resources.

ECON 470.description: Professional Research in Economics and Data Science. Delve into data science through industry led projects with real data. Develop effective communication skills and production-grade coding.

ECON 474.description: Economic Consulting and Applied Managerial Economics. Economic consulting and managerial economic methods applied in real world problems. Economic methods to analyze issues of intellectual property, environmental damage, trademark infringement, brand value, and consumer demand.

ECON 480.description: Economics of Industrial Organization. Pricing and resource allocation in imperfectly competitive         markets; monopoly regulation, collusion, cartels, mergers and      antitrust; patents and development incentives; industry case       studies.

ECON 487.description: Resource and Environmental Economics. Management and extraction of renewable and non-renewable natural   resources; environmental externalities and regulation of air,      water, and land pollution; market incentives versus direct         regulation.

ECON 490.description: Directed Research. Supervised individual research. Not available for graduate credit. Requires departmental approval.

ECON 495.description: Honors Thesis. Individual research supervised by a faculty advisor. Successful completion required for departmental honors degree.

ECON 499.description: Special Topics. Selected topics in economic theory, history, or policy.

ECON 500.description: Microeconomic Analysis and Policy. Theories of the household and the firm; product and factor markets; perfect and imperfect competition; welfare criteria.

ECON 501.description: Macroeconomic Analysis and Policy. Theories of aggregate economic activity; design and use of macroeconometric models; stabilization and control of inflation, unemployment, and growth.

ECON 504.description: Game Theory with Economic and Financial Applications. Applying game theory to economic and financial markets and interactions in a diverse set of examples like reputation, herding, bubbles and crashes, auctions, strategic information revelation and information accumulation in markets. Witnessing the wide range of applications that is amenable to game theoretical analysis.

ECON 513.description: Practice of Econometrics. Application of econometric tools using standard econometric software packages for microcomputers; empirical applications to selected economic problems of estimation and inference.

ECON 515.description: Time Series Analysis. Understanding and implementing models commonly used in time series econometrics. Emphasis is placed on intuition and application. Assists students understanding how to use time series data to test hypotheses and serve as an introduction to the ideas and techniques of forecasting.

ECON 521.description: International Macroeconomics and Financial Policy. The balance of payments, macroeconomic policy in an open economy, exchange rate determination, exchange rate systems, currency crises, international financial arrangements and monetary history.

ECON 550.description: Applied Trade Policy. Introduction and exploration of quantitative methods and data sources used for applied trade policy analysis.

ECON 555.description: Topics in Asset Pricing Theory. How do investors evaluate risks? With what information? How do they form their beliefs? Via empirical evidence and theoretical works, this course addresses these questions.

ECON 569.description: Cryptoeconomics and Blockchain Mechanisms. Introduction to the economics of decentralized blockchain systems; explores how mechanism design and cryptography are used in combination to build secure, trustless, consensus-driven blockchains

ECON 570.description: Big Data Econometrics. Introduction to the theory and practice of causal econometrics in modern settings of large-scale data. Major algorithms from machine learning focused on methodology and applications.

ECON 571.description: Economics of Digital Platforms. Introduces the novel business model and important features associated with digital platforms and analyzes firms various competitive behavior and anticompetitive conducts in the digital space.

ECON 577.description: Foundations of Financial Economics. Broad training in theoretical and empirical finance. Choice under uncertainty; equilibrium asset pricing; static portfolio choice; factor pricing models, asset allocation; the Black-Scholes-Merton Formula.

ECON 580.description: Antitrust Economics and Competition Policy. Efficiency, market failure, government regulation, some basics for antitrust economics, competition policy analysis and collusion and agreements among competitors.

ECON 584.description: Economic Consulting and Applied Econometrics. Economic methods to analyze issues of intellectual property, environmental damage, trademark infringement, brand value and consumer demand, using an applied econometric approach.

ECON 590.description: Directed Research.  Research leading to the master's degree. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

ECON 596.description: Internship for Curricular Practical Training. Part-time or full-time, practical work experience in the student's  field of study. Students must have a specific job/internship  offer. Job must be related to students major. The internship must  be located at an off-campus facility. Students are individually  supervised by faculty. Students must have been in F-1 student  status for at least one academic year in a degree-seeking program  before they can apply for CPT, with a cumulative 3.0 GPA. Course  does not apply to degree credit. Open only to graduate students.

ECON 603.description: Microeconomic Theory II. General equilibrium theory; existence, uniqueness, and stability; welfare economics; social choice; dynamic models and uncertainty; special topics. Prerequisite: ECON-601.

ECON 605.description: Macroeconomic Theory II. Macroeconomic theory based on the concepts of optimal growth and intertemporal equilibrium; overlapping generations models; recent developments in macroeconomic theory. Prerequisites: ECON-601 and ECON-602.

ECON 609.description: Econometric Methods. Review of statistical methods of estimation and inference, linear regression with multicollinearity and serial correlation; multivariate regression and simultaneous equations. Prerequisite: ECON 611. Duplicates credit in former ECON 511.

ECON 616.description: Experimental Economics. Laboratory methods for testing economic theory; experimental comparison of alternative market and non-market institutions; identification of behavioral responses to alternative regulations.

ECON 641.description: Empirical Analysis of Economic Development. Theory and empirics of the sources of and barriers to economic development and the micro underpinnings of macroeconomic dynamics of growth, inequality, and productivity. Prerequisites: ECON 601 and ECON 609.

ECON 661.description: Topics in Macroeconomics. Current areas of research in macroeconomics: Structural Change; Inequality and Macroeconomics.

ECON 681.description: Economics of Regulated Industries. Theories and methods of government regulation; effects of regulation on various industries; behavior of regulatory agencies. Prerequisites: ECON-500 or ECON-601.

ECON 686B.description: Empirical Methods in Economics     . Think about and design empirical studies in economics using cutting-edge approaches to causal inference -- structural and discrete choice models, micro-macro models and historical data models.

ECON 690.description: Seminar in Economic Theory. Current research in economic theory presented by faculty, students, and outside scholars. Graded CR/NC.

ECON 691.description: Seminar in Econometrics. Current research in econometrics presented by faculty, students, and outside scholars. Graded CR/NC.

ECON 693.description: Seminar in Applied Economics and Public Policy. Current research in applied microeconomics, macroeconomics, and public policy presented by faculty, students, and outside scholars. Graded CR/NC.

ECON 694.description: Seminar in Dynamic Economics. Graded CR/NC.

ECON 696.description: Empirical Microeconomics Seminar. Presentations on current research in empirical microeconomics by  outstanding scholars from leading Economics departments and  faculty at USC.  Open only to Economics Ph.D. students.  Graded  CR/NC.

ECON 700.description: Research on Frontier Economics. Examination of various frontier research topics of economics through critical discussions of research papers that study the most recent economic research agendas.

ECON 715.description: Advanced Topics in Econometrics. Time-series methods; aggregation; structural models and methods such as factor analysis and multiple indicator models; various special topics.

EDUC 547.description: Career Development: Theory and Process. Theories and process of career development; principles of career and leisure planning and counseling applicable throughout life.

EDUC 611.description: Athletic Administration. Analysis and discussion of critical issues in intercollegiate  athletics. Student-athlete academic and social accountability;  challenges of NCAA policies; commercialization, marketing, and  fundraising in college athletics.

EDUC 623.description: Understanding Research That Informs Leadership. Understanding, interpreting, and applying education research. Open only to doctoral students.

EDUC 627.description: Education Performance Problems: Role of Learning. Contemporary perspectives on learning and motivation. Strategies and tools for identifying, diagnosing, and solving learning and motivational challenges and opportunities.

EDUC 629.description: Consulting Practicum Context Analysis. Preparation, design and analysis of an education-related problem.

EDUC 630.description: Organizations and Policy: Current Issues. Study of contemporary issues in educational organizations, policy  and change in K-12 and higher education with an explicit focus on  the improvement of urban education.  Open to students admitted to  the Ph.D. only.

EDUC 634.description: Couples Counseling                 . Examination of relational development and change, strategies for  intervention with couples, and selected issues in couples  relational functioning.

EDUC 635.description: Psychotherapy with Children and Adolescents. Training in unique diagnostic considerations in working with children and adolescents. Exposure to empirically supported treatment modalities for children and adolescents.

EDUC 645B.description: Practicum II. Supervised practicum experience in a clinical setting.

EDUC 646.description: Marriage and Family Therapy Capstone:  Leadership Project. Culminating academic, professional and reflective experience for MFT candidates in their final year.  Students will identify and address issues of professional and clinical practice.

EDUC 652.description: Inquiry Methods III. Logic and methods of qualitative data analysis in the examination of educational issues and the framing of solutions for them.

EDUC 653.description: Qualitative Methods 2. Interactive seminar that explores the theoretical underpinnings and practicalities of interviews, portraiture, focus groups, life histories, and cultural biographies.

EDUC 663.description: Race and Racism in Education. Race, racism, racial equity, Critical Race Theory (CRT) will be explored particularly within educational institutions, with a heavy focus placed on practice.

EDUC 667.description: Racism and Anti-Blackness in Education. A holistic understanding of the historical underpinnings, persistent pathways and contemporary pillars of racism and white supremacy in education.

EDUC 681.description: Research, Policy and Practice in Urban Education. Development of urban education through the social, historical and political lens as it shapes and influences education research and policy.

EDUE 560.description: Identity and Diversity. Explore the historical and contemporary foundations of hierarchies and relationships of power, sociocultural diversity of experiences and sociopolitical resistance within higher education.

EDUE 676.description: Context of Organizational Change. External factors impacting organizations; human-centered organizational design;  evidence-based decision-making for thriving in dynamic environments.

EDUE 683.description: Quantitative Method and Data Analysis for Education. Develop skills to critically assess and apply quantitative research. Explore equitable approaches through systematic collection and analysis of data, utilizing standardized tools and statistical analysis.

EDUE 684.description: Advanced Theories in Mental Health Practice. Apply advanced clinical, counseling and psychotherapy concepts into leadership practice. Emphasis on cultural humility, evidenced-based practice, marginalized communities and self-exploration.

EDUE 689.description: Consultation, Program Development and Evaluation. Acquire skills to design, implement and assess evaluation studies and consult with other mental health organizations. Focus on cultural humility via program design and evaluation.

EDUE 692.description: Current and Emerging Opportunities in Leadership. Identification and analysis of current and emerging leadership opportunities and global and systemic challenges in the context of advancing human-centered organizations.

EDUE 698.description: Qualitative Methods and Analysis. Qualitative research methods for practitioner scholars; systematic qualitative data collection, analysis and interpretation.

EDUE 702.description: Foundations in Learning. Supports the development of critically conscious leaders who facilitate learning in urban contexts by understanding how culture, identity and power influence learners' opportunities to learn.

EDUE 703.description: Power, Diversity and Equity. Explores power, diversity and equity through the social, historical, and political lenses as these constructs shape and impact education (P-20) research, policy and professional practice.

EDUE 704.description: Leadership Enactment. Provides students with the opportunity to acquire or deepen knowledge and skills related to acting as a critically conscious leaders who address existing educational inequities.

EDUE 707.description: Advanced Clinical Topics. Explore specialized clinical topics in mental health, emphasizing practical application and employee skill development in crisis intervention, trauma treatment, grant writing, budgeting and professional communication.

EDUE 709.description: Facilitating Learning, Motivation and Wellbeing. Evidence-based strategies to promote employee engagement and well-being in organizational contexts; inclusive policies and practices that facilitate employee motivation, learning and development.

EDUE 710.description: Designing Educational Organizations for Equity. Introduction to organizational theory and design with emphasis on building and leading organizations based on the principles of equity and social justice.

EDUE 721.description: Proseminar in Career Development in Mental Health Leadership. Acquire leadership skills for diverse mental health settings, emphasizing values-driven leadership, critical self-reflection and mindful communication for individual self-care and organizational well-being.

EDUE 727.description: Research Methods 2. Building on Research Methods 1, students learn to implement a research design by conducting pilot studies to answer quantitative and qualitative research questions.

EDUE 728.description: Leadership of Site and System Organizational Learning. Applying leadership theory and adult learning theory to real-world challenges facing school and district leaders.

EE 105.description: Introduction to Electrical Engineering. Electrical engineering overview: communications, computers, circuits, components, signals, electromagnetics, microelectronics; data encoding and compression, USPS and UPC product codes, DVDs, semiconductor devices, and integrated circuits.

EE 109.description: Introduction to Embedded Systems. Information representations, embedded programming, digital and serial I/O, analog-to-digital conversion, and interrupt mechanisms. Elementary analog, logic and state-machine design.

EE 141.description: Applied Linear Algebra for Engineering. Introduction to linear algebra with engineering applications.  Weekly laboratory exercises using MATLAB.

EE 155.description: Introduction to Computer Programming for         Electrical Engineers                            . Introduction to solving engineering problems using computational methods.  Survey of various programming languages and their strengths and weaknesses.  Program structure, input/output, conditionals, loops, functions, arrays.

EE 202.description: Linear Circuits. Lumped circuit elements; network equations; zero-input and zerostate responses; sinusoidal steady-state analysis; impedance; resonance; network functions; power concepts; transformers; Laplace transforms.

EE 250.description: Distributed Systems for the Internet of Things. Introduction to hardware, operating systems, signal processing and control, network protocols, mobile applications, databases, cloud computing, machine learning and security for the Internet of Things.

EE 301.description: Linear Systems. Representation and analysis of linear time-invariant systems primarily for the continuous time case. Convolution, Fourier series and transform, Laplace transform, controls and communications applications.

EE 354.description: Digital Circuits. Digital system design and implementation; synchronous design of datapath and control; schematic/Verilog-based design, simulation, and implementation in Field Programmable Gate Arrays; timing analysis; semester-end project.

EE 355.description: Software Design for Electrical Engineers. Object-oriented programming techniques, basic data structures and elementary complexity analysis for the modeling, simulation and solution of engineering problems.

EE 364.description: Probability and Statistics for Engineers and Computer Scient. Introduction to concepts of randomness and uncertainty: probability, random variables, statistics. Applications to digital communications, signal processing, automatic control, computer engineering and computer science.

EE 370.description: Electromagnetics for Engineering Systems. Electromagnetic plane-wave propagation and interactions with simple media, transmission/reception of wireless signals in complex environments. Optimization design methods for system applications.

EE 443.description: Power Systems. Components of power systems; analysis techniques in electrical power generation transmission and utilization; and environmental and economic considerations in system operations and planning.

EE 448.description: Communication Electronics. Analysis, design, and experimental evaluation of transistor-level  communication circuits and micro-systems.  Transmission lines,  impedance matching, noise, distortion, tuned amplifiers, mixers,  oscillators, phase-locked loops.

EE 459.description: Embedded Systems Design Laboratory. Specification, design, implementation, testing and documentation of a digital system project using embedded processors, programmable logic, analog I/O interfaces and application specific hardware. Capstone design experience.

EE 460.description: Machine Learning for Engineers. Overview of machine learning, regression and classification, clustering and dimensionality reduction, loss-functions, over/under-fitting, cross-validation, kernel machines, decision trees and neural networks.

EE 467.description: Fundamentals of Communication Systems. Broad treatment of analog and digital communication systems. Modulation and demodulation techniques using a carrier wave's amplitude, frequency, phase. Channel signal and noise. Review current systems.

EE 477.description: MOS VLSI Circuit Design. Analysis and design of digital MOS VLSI circuits including area, delay and power minimization. Laboratory assignments including design, layout, extraction, simulation and automatic synthesis.

EE 482.description: Linear Control Systems. Analysis of linear time-invariant (LTI) control systems; stability of LTI systems; frequency response, proportional-integral-differential (PID) and root-locus compensation techniques.

EE 501.description: Solid State. Atomic electronic states, molecular bonding, crystal structures, diffraction, reciprocal lattice, Brillouin zones, crystal binding, lattice vibrations, specific heat, anharmonic effects, energy bands, metals, conductivity.

EE 503.description: Probability for Electrical and Computer Engineers. Rigorous coverage of probability, discrete and continuous random variables, functions of multiple random variables, covariance, correlation, random sequences, Markov chains, estimation, and introduction to statistics. Duplicates credit in former EE 464 and EE 465.

EE 506.description: Semiconductor Physics. Semiconductor bonds, crystallography, band structure assumptions, group theory, band structure results, k.p. method, quantum wells, wires and dots, superlattices, amorphous, organic semiconductors, defects, statistics, surfaces.

EE 508.description: Hardware Foundations of Machine Learning. Introduction to ML accelerators; memory access kernels; parallelization approaches to the design of scalable ML systems; distributed ML; privacy in machine learning.

EE 510.description: Linear Algebra for Engineering. Introduction to linear algebra and matrix theory and their underlying concepts; applications to engineering problems; mathematically rigorous and foundational to other classes in communication, control, and signal processing.

EE 512.description: Stochastic Processes for Financial Engineering. Theory and applications of stochastic processes relevant to financial engineering. Stochastic processes, Brownian motion, martingales, stochastic calculus, Monte Carlo Simulations with financial application examples.

EE 515.description: Quantum Sensing: Machine Learning, Inference and Information. Basics of quantum mechanics, quantum sensing, quantum theory of inference, information and machine learning.

EE 518.description: Mathematics and Tools for Financial Engineering. Students will build a mathematical background for studying Financial Engineering. Emphasis is on analysis, proofs and examples. Mathworks Financial toolbox will be introduced.
