IR 101.description: International Relations.  Basic concepts of world affairs for non-majors. Development ofcompetency to understand and critically evaluate global relationsand international events, stressing empirical approaches. Not available for major credit.

IR 210.description: International Relations: Introductory Analysis. Comprehensive introduction to contending theoretical and analytical approaches; development of critical, evaluative, cognitive, and analytical competencies regarding historical and contemporary issues.

IR 211.description: International Relations: Approaches to Research. Introduction to theoretically oriented research approaches and designs; emphasis on the logic of argumentation.

IR 213.description: The Global Economy. Economic and political concepts necessary to the understanding of the modern global economy. Topics include international trade, foreign investment and migration.

IR 303.description: Leadership and Diplomacy. The role of leaders, diplomatic leadership and creativity in  statecraft, providing a deep understanding of the theoretical and  practical dimensions of diplomacy.

IR 304.description: National Intelligence and the Shaping of Policy. The focus is intelligence to improve the making of policy, with attention to collection; overt and covert, operations; domestic intelligence; and oversight in democracies.

IR 305.description: Managing New Global Challenges. Examines the strategies for managing global issues in the post Cold War period. Explores ways that international institutions, national governments and non-state actors work separately and together to provide order and control over complex international issues areas. Issues that will receive attention could include financial and monetary relations, trade and foreign investment, preservation of the environment, the spread of weapons of mass destruction, population and migration, terrori

IR 306.description: International Organizations. The emergence of international organizations as a permanent feature in world politics; role of the United Nations Organization as well as regional international organizations.

IR 308.description: Economic Globalization. Globalization makes national borders and regulations increasingly obsolete. Analyzes the economic foundation of globalization, its consequences and efforts to manage it.

IR 310.description: Peace and Conflict Studies. Interdisciplinary study of the pursuit of peace, including causes of wars, arms races, conflict resolution, peace movements, nonviolent resistance, and peace with justice.

IR 313.description: Religions and Political Violence. An introduction to debates about the intersection of religion and conflict in politics and international affairs; theoretical, classical, and contemporary issues.

IR 319.description: Human Security and Humanitarian Intervention. Explore causes of human security, international  responses to issues like violence, displacement and climate change; and the costs, benefits and effects of humanitarian intervention.

IR 321.description: Civil War, Peace Building and International Intervention. Examination of the causes of civil war, the dynamics and consequences of civil war and how peace is or is not built.

IR 325.description: North-South Relations in the Global Economy.  Analysis of inequality in relations between developed and developing states; contending views on the causes and legacies of imperialism; development strategies and aid.

IR 329.description: The Global Finance and Monetary Regime. The international financial and monetary regime, its evolution and the problems facing it today

IR 330.description: Politics of the World Economy. Exploration of questions and concepts in international economics and politics, especially as they relate to flows of trade, capital, people, and problems across borders.

IR 343.description: U.S. Foreign Policy Since World War II.  Analysis of U.S. foreign policy since 1945 as a basis for understanding significant new trends. Explanation of contemporary issues in U.S. relations with other nations.

IR 344.description: The Global South in World Politics. Origin, concepts, realities and ideals of the non-aligned movement, focusing on the role of the United States in the developing world.

IR 345.description: Russian and Post-Soviet Foreign Policy. Overview of Tsarist and Soviet experience as background to detailed examination of the political, economic and ideological forces behind contemporary Russian foreign policy.

IR 357.description: Urban Politics in the Global South. Examination of social and economic justice in the questions of urban governance facing cities in the developing world.

IR 362.description: The International Relations of the Contemporary Middle East.  Introduction to problems and issues in the Middle East today: religio-ethnic rivalries, conflicting nationalisms and ideologies, the Arab-Israeli conflict, Middle East oil.

IR 364.description: The Political Economy of Latin American Development. The main economic development themes and strategies in Latin  America over the past century.  The interplay between domestic and  international variables, and the resulting dynamic changes.

IR 365.description: Politics and Democracy in Latin America. Examines Latin America's experience with democracy emphasizing  events since the 1980s.  Analyzes the roles of interest groups,  ideology, domestic politics, bureaucratic processes, perceptions  and analogical reasoning.

IR 371.description: Global Civil Society: Non-State Actors in World Politics. Examination of diplomatic and moral relationships between sovereign states and transnational non-state actors, both benevolent (humanitarian groups and philanthropies) and malevolent (mercenaries, pirates and terrorists).

IR 381.description: Introduction to International Security. Key concepts in international security studies; historical evolution of international warfare and diplomacy; contemporary international security issues.

IR 386.description: Terrorism and Counterterrorism. Examination of terrorism and responses to terrorism, including how societies understand and deal with terrorism; focus on ethical and normative issues.

IR 391.description: Directed International Relations Field Study. Intensive internship experience in international relations professional areas with academic research component (may be repeated for credit different semesters)

IR 397.description: Field Research in Human Rights. Conducting human rights research and policy work in the field

IR 402.description: Theories of War. Causes of war; means of prevention and consequences of war.

IR 413.description: Applied Data Science for International Relations 2. Intermediate statistical computing and data visualization in R. Focus the on graphical presentation of complex statistical relationships. Students create publication-ready figures for actual faculty research projects.

IR 420.description: Political Economy of Corruption. Examines causes, consequences and how to combat corruption as an economic, political and social problem.

IR 425.description: The New Triangle: China, the U.S. and Latin America. China's rise in the international political economy raises policy research questions, including an analysis of how this trend relates to U.S and Latin American relations. Recommended preparation: Micro and macro economics

IR 427.description: Seminar on Economics and Security. Introduction to important economic issue areas that are understood as security-related in the contemporary world: population, food, trade, debt, etc.

IR 490.description: Directed Research.  Individual research and readings. Not available for graduate credit.

IR 499.description: Special Topics.  Selected topics in various special areas within international relations, which may vary from semester to semester or within semesters.

ITAL 120.description: Italian I.  Introduction to current Italian. Oral practice, hearing and reading comprehension; grammar necessary for simple spoken and written expression. Lecture, classroom drill, laboratory drill.

ITAL 150.description: Italian II. Continuation of Italian I.

ITAL 175.description: Accelerated Italian for Speakers of Spanish and  Other Romance Languages                         . Accelerated introduction to written and spoken Italian for students with a high level of proficiency in Spanish or another Romance Language.  Students completing this course may enroll in the third semester of the basic language sequence ITAL 220.

ITAL 220.description: Italian III. Continuation of Italian II. Review of structure of the language, drill in aural and reading comprehension, practice in oral expression.

ITAL 222.description: Italian Professional Internship: Communication and Culture. Combined classroom discussion and supervised internship at companies. Practical experience in applying communication and cultural knowledge in a professional employment context.

ITAL 240.description: Italian IV. Continuation of Italian III.  Review and expand upon abilities to create with the language in concrete exchanges, descriptions, comparisons, questions and discussions relevant to current issues and topics.

ITAL 360.description: Italian Cinema. Survey of Italian cinema in its relation to social transformation, from the silent era to the present. Weekly screenings, lectures, and discussions. Conducted in English.

ITAL 490.description: Directed Research.  Individual research and readings. Not available for graduate credit.

MUJZ 150.description: Beginning Jazz Improvisation. Development of beginning improvisational skills including underlying principles of theory, harmony, jazz ear training, and jazz style.

MUJZ 153.description: Individual Instruction. Weekly individual instructio and performance forum.  Open only to  jazz studies majors.

MUJZ 195.description: Jazz Elements I. Study of compositional, improvisational, performance, and  arranging elements found in jazz.  Students will model influential  groups and jazz artists.

MUJZ 218A.description: Afro-Latin Percussion Instruments. Instruction in the performance of percussion instruments associated with African, South American, and Caribbean music traditions, with special emphasis on adaptation to jazz music.

MUJZ 218B.description: Afro-Latin Percussion Instruments. Instruction in the performance of percussion instruments associated with African, South American, and Caribbean music traditions, with special emphasis on adaptation to jazz music.

MUJZ 253.description: Individual Instruction. Weekly individual instruction and performance forum.  Open only to  jazz studies majors.

MUJZ 300.description: Non-Major Individual Instruction. Intermediate and advanced instruction designed for non-music  majors.  Not available for credit to music majors.

MUJZ 301.description: Individual Instruction. Intermediate and advanced instruction on secondary instrument for  music majors, on principal instrument for music minors and B.S.  music majors.  Open only to music majors and minors.

MUJZ 305B.description: Advanced Jazz Theory. Analysis and transcription of jazz performances and scores,  encompassing questions of style, form, harmonic and melodic  language, and considerations of rhythm.

MUJZ 350.description: A History of Jazz Music. A history of jazz music and the styles of music considered antecedents to jazz.

MUJZ 353.description: Individual Instruction. Weekly individual instruction and performance forum.  Open only to  jazz studies majors.

MUJZ 395.description: Jazz Elements II. Advanced study of compositional, improvisational, performance, conducting, and arranging elements found in the jazz repertory. Students will be encouraged to forge individual musical expressions.

MUJZ 400.description: Arranging for Jazz Ensemble.  Scoring for jazz ensemble with emphasis on writing for sections of like and mixed instruments as well as full ensemble.

MUJZ 450.description: Intermediate Jazz Improvisation. Development of intermediate improvisational skills including underlying principles of theory, harmony, jazz ear training, and jazz style. Recommended preparation: MUJZ 150.

MUJZ 453.description: Individual Instruction. Weekly individual instruction and performance forum.  Open only to  jazz studies majors.

MUJZ 490.description: Directed Research.  Individual research and readings. No available for graduate credit.

MUJZ 501.description: Individual Instruction. Secondary instruction for graduate music majors or instruction for  graduate non-music majors.

MUJZ 536.description: Jazz Composition for Orchestra. Jazz Composition skills using symphonic instrumentation; Listening assignments provide technique and historical perspective. Scoring assignments for orchestra with rhythm section, and smaller instrument combinations.

MUJZ 551.description: Graduate Jazz Improvisation. Development of proficiency in improvising to advanced jazz  concepts, including transposition, substitute harmony,  superimposed harmony, atypical harmonic schemes, and contemporary  chord and scale types.  Open to jazz studies majors and studio  guitar majors.

MUJZ 554.description: Graduate Certificate Performance. Individual instruction and related lab participation for Graduate  Certificate students.

MUJZ 590.description: Directed Research.  Research leading to the Master's Degree. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

MUJZ 653.description: Performance.  Individual or master class instruction for D.M.A. Performance majors.

MUJZ 790.description: Research. Research leading to the doctorate.  Maximum units which may be  applied to the degree to be determined by the department.  Graded  CR/NC.

JOUR 200.description: The Power and Responsibility of the Press. Explores the role of journalism and social media in society - its influence on government, technology, business, national security, sports, science and entertainment.

JOUR 201.description: Culture of Journalism: Past, Present and Future. Examines the social, cultural and political aspects of U.S. journalism over time and currently.

JOUR 205.description: Journalism Practicum. Field experience in journalism, public relations, or related field.

JOUR 206.description: Reporting and Writing Practicum. Experiential lab in which students report, write and produce digital journalism content and report and produce live radio/television broadcasts in a student-led newsroom.

JOUR 207.description: Reporting and Writing I. Journalism fundamentals, including news judgment,  finding and verifying information, and reporting and writing.

JOUR 210.description: Basics of News Production for Non-Majors. Introduction to television, radio, and/or digital news production. Examination of issues in journalism.

JOUR 307.description: Reporting and Writing II. Report, write, produce and distribute in-depth stories, including longer news and analysis pieces.

JOUR 320.description: Introduction to Coding for Storytelling. Introduction to basic web technologies; conceive, design, code and produce an advanced multimedia story package.

JOUR 321.description: Visual Journalism. Basics of visual journalism, including video storytelling and photography.

JOUR 322.description: Introduction to Investigative and Data Journalism. Reportorial and analytical skills and techniques required for portraying and evaluating contemporary newsworthy events using basic data journalism techniques and tools for statistical analysis.

JOUR 330.description: Photojournalism. Emphasis on fundamental skills necessary for photojournalism  including camera techniques, story ideas and digital darkroom.

JOUR 340.description: Rewriting History: Reporting Rome. Develop reporting skills by studying historical unsolved Italian crimes. Visit crime scenes, examine evidence, interview sources, analyze media reports and write articles for each crime.

JOUR 350.description: Introduction to Sports Media. Highlight norms, routines of content, including print, broadcast, video. Focus on opportunities, constraints posed by roles of reporters, fans, players, publicists, agents, leagues, teams.

JOUR 372.description: Engaging Diverse Communities. Covers strategies of community engagement and beat reporting.

JOUR 381.description: Entertainment, Business and Media in Today's Society. An examination of the symbiotic relationship of the entertainment  business and the media; press coverage of the entertainment  industry; Hollywood's relationship with news media.

JOUR 403.description: Television News and Sports Production. Production of television news and sports programs while developing video, writing and communication skills and managing content in collaboration with others under deadline pressure.

JOUR 404.description: Produce and Host Sports Content in Studio A. Interview, present and design sports segments for television/video in Studio A.

JOUR 405.description: Non-Fiction Television. Presentation and selection in non-fiction television programs including documentaries, electronic magazines and news series; ethical problems, field research, reporting, interviewing, pre-production.

JOUR 409.description: Audio Storytelling for Radio and Podcast. Techniques for audio journalism, including effective use of sound, art of the interview, writing for the ear and crafting stories to engage listeners.

JOUR 414.description: Advanced Digital Media Storytelling. An advanced single-topic multimedia package.

JOUR 430.description: Writing the Film Review. Techniques of writing the film review; preparation and treatment of form and content; problems, responsibilities and ethics of film reviewing.

JOUR 432.description: Sports Commentary. Techniques of reporting and writing sports columns and commentary for print, video, radio and Web-based media.

JOUR 441.description: Sports Reporting. News and feature coverage of sporting events, including social and economic factors influencing sports in America.

JOUR 446.description: Entertainment Reporting. Techniques of reporting and writing about the entertainment business, economics and finances. Analysis of the skills and background needed for reporters specializing in this area of the news.

JOUR 447.description: Arts Reporting. Techniques of reporting and writing about the arts, including television, film, theatre, music, graphic arts, architecture and design.

JOUR 457.description: Food of Our Families. Tell stories that explore food culture and culinary traditions, become familiar with cultural areas of Los Angeles and become immersed in global food and culture.

JOUR 462.description: Law of Mass Communication. Covers the First Amendment and case law establishing journalists' freedoms and providing the framework for the practice of the craft.

JOUR 475.description: Print and Digital Design for 21st Century Storytelling. Art, typography, and other graphic elements in publication design; traditional, contemporary, and advanced production methods, processes, and equipment; representative examples; practice in design.

JOUR 480.description: Sports and Media Technology. Examine and analyze the ever-changing technology sector of the sports business and sports media worlds. Identify emerging technologies being developed in the sports industry and how they are being utilized to enhance the fan experience.

JOUR 490.description: Directed Research.  Individual research and readings. Not available for graduate credit.

JOUR 491.description: News Leadership. Brutal economics, labor-management tensions, DEI, lawsuit threats -- learn how news leaders juggle all this and more while inspiring their staff to produce great journalism.

JOUR 499.description: Special Topics.  Selected topics in journalism.

JOUR 522.description: Video Documentary Production. Production of video documentary including research and reporting techniques, writing, interviewing, field work, editing, legal issues, economics, aesthetics, balanced presentation, ethics, diversity and production problems.

JOUR 524.description: Advanced Video Reporting. Reporting, production and writing for broadcast and other video platforms; practical experience; role of the video broadcast journalist; similarities and differences between media.

JOUR 525.description: This California Life: Storytelling for Radio and Podcasting. Advanced production techniques for public radio-style reports: writing, sound, editing, narrative voice. Techniques applicable for broadcast features or Web audio documentaries.

JOUR 527.description: Advanced Disruption: Innovation with Emerging Technology. Apply emerging technologies to tell innovative stories based on a production trip during spring break.

JOUR 542.description: Foreign Affairs Reporting. News stories analyzed, researched, and critiqued for validity and background; projects to include editorials, news stories, magazine articles or broadcast reports.

JOUR 547.description: Navigating the Media Marketplace. Explores the economics of the news industry and prepares students to navigate the journalism job market through practical exercises, practice interviews and cover letter-writing.

JOUR 557.description: Digital Investigations II: OSINT Reporting Lab. Advanced techniques in open-source investigations and investigative reporting. Group research and publication of stories on important current topics grounded in digital investigations.

JOUR 569.description: The Art of (Macro) Food Journalism: A Global View. Food is a powerful lens for thinking about cities, community, climate, technology, culture - even our relationship to other species. Focus is on the global.

JOUR 572.description: Reporting on Entertainment and Popular Culture. Reporting about entertainment, popular culture and their impact on American society; survey of past media coverage and current practices.

JOUR 579.description: Journalism Internship. Field experience in journalism, public relations, or related field.

JOUR 585.description: Specialized Reporting: Religion. Reporting and writing on religion; survey of world religion, religion and public life-including politics, gender and science.

JOUR 590.description: Directed Research.  Research leading to the Master's degree. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

JOUR 593.description: Arts Criticism and Commentary. Writing workshops and independent fieldwork; development of critical skills to write socially valuable criticism and commentary about art, entertainment and culture.

JOUR 594B.description: Master's Thesis.  Credit on acceptance of thesis.

JOUR 598.description: Journalism Capstone Project. Production of a journalism capstone project with multimedia elements for a master's degree. Projects can be single stand-alone pieces, or series of pieces.

JS 100.description: Jewish History. Major ideas, personalities, and movements in Jewish history from antiquity to the present in light of the interaction of the Jews with the general culture.

JS 150.description: Jewish Histories of the Modern Middle East. Explores Jewish participation in the social, cultural, political and economic life of the modern Middle East.

JS 170.description: Exploring the Hebrew Bible. Exploring the Hebrew Bible, the world in which it arose, and influential texts, including work from Ancient Egypt, Mesopotamia  and the Southern Levant.

JS 180.description: Judaism. Jewish beliefs, practices, and history from the biblical period to the present; Judaic contributions to Western civilization.

JS 211.description: The Holocaust.  Historical background and responses to the Holocaust, withspecial emphasis on ethical implications.

JS 310.description: The Eastern European Jewish Experience: Literature and Film. Analyzes works by different artists -- writers, filmmakers, painters -- in order to understand the significant contribution that the Jewish experience in Eastern Europe has made to Jewish communities worldwide.

JS 402.description: Jews, Judaism and Race. Examine the history of race and racialization in Jewish life,  culture and history across the world and the impact of race on  Jewish tradition.

JS 415.description: The American Jewish Experience in Film. A survey of American Jewish history through the medium of film,  with particular emphasis on the experience of the post-war  generation.

JS 490.description: Directed Research.  Individual research and readings. Not available for graduate credit.

JS 590.description: Directed Research.  Research leading to the master's degree. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

LAT 120.description: Latin I. Essentials of Latin grammar and vocabulary.

LAT 150.description: Latin II. Essentials of Latin grammar and vocabulary, continued.  Basic  reading skills.

LAT 222.description: Latin III. Reading Latin literature.  Introduction to reading and translation  of classical Latin prose and poetry.  Extensive grammar review.

LAT 450.description: Readings in Latin Literature. Readings in various authors and genres of latin literature.

LAW 101.description: Law and the U.S. Constitution in Global History. By examining key constitutional moments involving race, rights, and revolutions, students will explore how legal meaning changes over time.

LAW 200.description: Law and Society. Sources and structure of law; history of Bill of Rights emphasizing effect on criminal justice system; limits of law in solving problems in American society.

LAW 201.description: Law and Politics. Examination of the rules and realities of American politics, and the role politics plays in American life and culture.

LAW 205.description: Introduction to Criminal Law. Provides a comprehensive analysis of the criminal justice system and an overview of the fundamentals of substantive criminal law.

LAW 210.description: Fundamentals of the U.S. Legal System. Introduces the U.S. legal system and its relationship to basic principles of the rule of law. Examines lawmaking institutions, judicial processes and contemporary legal issues.

LAW 211.description: Intellectual Property and Technology. Examines how American law protects and facilitates intellectual property and its modern utility. Provides a practical understanding of laws regulating patents, copyrights and trademarks.

LAW 212.description: Immigration Law for a New America. Examines current immigration law in America, the normative debates over immigration policies and the role the government plays in expanding or limiting immigration rights.

LAW 222.description: Interdisciplinary Perspectives on the Law. Examines law and the legal system from different disciplinary perspectives. It explores how various disciplines provide different insights to the legal regime.

LAW 223.description: Exploring Courthouses in Los Angeles. Gain hands-on experience by observing the inner workings of the criminal and civil law system through lectures and courtrooms visits.

LAW 225.description: Current Court Cases. Exposes students to the impact of legal decisions on society through analysis of pending and recent cases on the courts docket.

LAW 250.description: Children and the Law. Examines topics such as children's suggestibility, decision-making, and risk and resiliency all as they apply to legal settings.

LAW 300.description: Concepts in American Law. The main concepts and topics in American law, in the historical, economic and cultural contexts in which they have developed.

LAW 301.description: Voting Rights and the Law. Examines the basic themes surrounding the legal regulation of elections with a focus on voting rights.

LAW 310.description: Global Justice for Mass Atrocities and Genocide. Learn about international law and courts trying these cases, while also reflecting on whether criminal trials are the best response to bringing healing and reconciliation to affected societies.

LAW 311.description: Fundamentals of Entertainment Law. Examines key legal principles governing the entertainment industry by exploring legal challenges faced by professionals in music, film, sports, gaming and other areas of entertainment.

LAW 320.description: Law, Enslavement and Race. Studies how law, politics and culture interacted to shape the institution of enslavement and the development of modern conceptions of race.

LAW 324.description: Sports Law. Examines the relevance and application of legal structures to all participants in the sports enterprise by providing an overview of legal and ethical issues.

LAW 326.description: Law and the Modern Athlete. Covers legal frameworks that affect today's athletes and students working in sports: amateurism, negotiation, gambling, social media, agents and finding jobs in sports.

LAW 350.description: Law and Entrepreneurship. Examines areas of the law that impact entrepreneurs, starting, operating and financing businesses. Topics include: selection of business entities; securities laws and issues that arise in fundraising; employment law; contracts; torts; intellectual property; global expansion; mergers and acquisitions; and IPOs.

LAW 352.description: Introduction to Law and Economics. An exploration of core aspects of the US legal system (property, contracts, torts, criminal law, civil procedure) from the perspective of basic economics theory.

LAW 355.description: Law and Homelessness. Examines the current housing crisis by interweaving tenant/landlord law, local ordinances, historical exclusionary policies and reviewing current reporting and scholarship.

LAW 402.description: Psychology and Law. Explores issues of responsibility and credibility.  Intentional  and unintentional behavior.  Clinical biases.  Topics include  witness credibility, confessions, cults, hostages, battered  persons, and repressed memories.

LAW 403.description: Mental Health Law. Foundational legal and practice concepts at the intersection of law and psychology through three intersecting systems: the mental health, the criminal and the immigration systems.

LAW 406.description: Individual Rights in U.S. Constitutional Law. Explores the U.S. Bill of Rights and the limits that the Constitution imposes on the state majority's ability to impose its will on an individual.

LAW 407.description: Regulatory Law. Introduces legal and social ideas and issues surrounding regulatory law - how and why regulations are developed, along with the accountability and enforcement of regulations.

LAW 492.description: Undergraduate Law Review. Introduces students to the basics of legal writing and research, with a focus on legal scholarship and law review-type journal articles.

LAW 497.description: Legal Studies Capstone Project. A cumulative experience demonstrating a student's depth of knowledge in applying research and writing skills on examining the legal system.

LAW 498.description: Law Internship. Intensive law-related experience with a non-profit organization, public agency, government agency or private company.

LAW 518.description: Transactional Law Research. This course strengthens legal research skills in transactional  law, focusing on corporate finance, mergers, tax, and industry  reports through hands-on exercises and strategic methodologies.

LAW 532.description: Constitutional Law: Rights. Examines constitutional rights particularly ones protected under the Equal Protection/Due Process Clauses and related questions of judicial role and theories of interpretation.

LAW 550.description: Law for Business. A student-run periodical that publishes student-written and peer-edited  articles relevant to the intersection between law and business.

LAW 553.description: Legal Issues of AI in Media and Entertainment. Addresses evolving issues in using generative AI to produce commercial products and services relating to intellectual property rights such as copyright and trademark.

LAW 579.description: Global Regulatory Compliance. Introduction to regimes that regulate business practices on a global level and compliance of such regimes, such as Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, OECD Anti-Bribery Convention, and other regulations.

LAW 600.description: Taxation.  Federal tax statutes, technical issues and social problems involved in tax planning, tax litigation, and reform of the tax laws.

LAW 602.description: Criminal Procedure. Criminal procedure in the courts, and the regulation of lawenforcement by the courts through rules of evidence andinterpretation of the Bill of Rights.

LAW 603.description: Business Organizations. Organization of economic activity especially the modern corporation as institutions of social power. The roles of managers, owners, and regulatory agencies in shaping processes ofdecision making.

LAW 607.description: Gifts, Wills, and Trusts.  Gratuitous transfer of wealth, especially the transmission of wealth from one generation to the next as a settlement of family affairs. Comparative analysis of the legal mechanisms of gifts, wills, and trusts. Introduction to problems of fiduciary administration.

LAW 608.description: Evidence. The purpose and character of trial. Problems of adversary presentation and the nature of proof. The basis for admission and exclusion of evidence in judicial proceedings.

LAW 612.description: California Civil Procedure. Examines the California rules of civil procedure. Emphasizes  California law, with some discussion of the differences between  state and federal procedure.

LAW 614.description: Accounting for Lawyers. The lawyer's skills needed to understand the financial affairs of a business client.

LAW 626.description: International Investment Law and Arbitration. Examine the protection offered to foreign investors through international investment agreements, which includes recourse to arbitration against the host states.

LAW 631.description: Mediation Clinic II. Continuation of LAW-630

LAW 636.description: Labor Law. The interrelation of labor, business, and government in collective bargaining, federal regulation of union and management practices and pressures, especially through the Taft-Hartley Act.

LAW 644.description: Corporate Taxation.  Tax principles and practice applicable to business, especially problems of formation, liquidation, and reorganization.

LAW 645.description: Transactional Practice - The Syndicated Loan Agreement. Involves issues including loan restructuring; what loan agreements cover; how representations, covenants, default and financial and repayment terms interrelate; and how security documents fit in. Graded CR/D/F.

LAW 648.description: Topics in Entertainment Law. Contemporary topics in the field of entertainment law.

LAW 652.description: Computer Crime Law. Examines the legal and policy issues involved with the emergence of cyber crimes and cyber security issues, including government access and privacy issues.

LAW 658.description: Mergers and Acquisitions. Problems of integrating the corporate, securities, tax, business,  antitrust, accounting and contractual aspects of corporate mergers and aquisitions.

LAW 659.description: Land use and Development Law. A practice-oriented introduction to various elements of land use  and real estate development law.

LAW 666B.description: Trademark Moot Court. An intensive, two-semester course preparing students interested in U.S. trademark and unfair competition law for participation in the annual Saul Lefkowitz Moot Court Competition.

LAW 668.description: Hale Moot Court Oral Advocacy. Invitation-only course for students in the Hale Moot Court Honors  Program.  Students present an oral argument and judge first-year  student rounds.  Graded CR/NC.

LAW 669.description: Moot Court Supervision. Evaluation and supervision of the preparation of briefs and oral arguments in the Hale Moot Court honors competition.

LAW 670.description: Advanced Moot Court Oral Arguments. Preparation of oral arguments in approved moot court competitions, such as national and state prize rounds, (other than Hale Moot Court Program).  Graded CR/69/65.  Open only to law students.

LAW 671.description: Advanced Moot Court Briefs. Preparation of briefs in approved moot court competitions, such as national and state prize rounds (other than Hale Moot Court Program).

LAW 683.description: Fact Investigation and Discovery. Introduction to a practice-oriented approach to interviewing and counseling clients. Enables students to develop a useful framework for effectively interviewing and representing clients.

LAW 685.description: The Modern U.S. Supreme Court. Examines the contemporary U.S. Supreme Court: the Court's membership; its procedures for selecting cases for review; the role of lawyers, law clerks and journalists; and doctrinal developments.

LAW 686.description: Civil Rights Law. Gives students operational significance to the abstractions presented in the Constitutional Law courses by investigating civil rights litigation.

LAW 689.description: Digital Media Transactions. Focuses on the business, legal, and financial issues that relate to the creation, financing, and exploitation of digital media.

LAW 698.description: Equity and the Legal and Social Determinants of Health. Explores how legal, social, racial, cultural and economic factors contribute to health disparities and the role that physicians and lawyers can play in advocating for patients and policy changes to promote health equity.

LAW 701.description: Child Interviewing Practicum. Learn how to effectively interview child witnesses. Students will practice mock interviews, and may be eligible to conduct actual interviews of child witnesses.

LAW 703A.description: Children's Legal Issues. Students will work on cases in the following areas: (1) Dependent and neglected children: All children who are wards of the court must have legal counsel. (2) Children with AIDS: Legal implications of such issues as health care and custody. (3) Guardianships or other temporary arrangements for children whose parents are terminally ill or are otherwise unable to care for them.

LAW 705.description: Community Property. The law of community property, including disposition of property on dissolution of the marriage and questions of conflict of laws.

LAW 707.description: Global Health, Law and Human Rights. Highlights the complex interactions between health, law and human rights, emphasizing the use of human rights in public health thinking and practice. Duplicates credit in PM-577.

LAW 709.description: Contract Drafting and Negotiation. Contract drafting and negotiating will teach students the   mechanics of drafting and negotiating sophisticated contracts from  a variety of legal disciplines including entertainment law, real  estate law and general corporate law.

LAW 710.description: Contract Drafting and Analysis. Students present to the class their assessment of assigned contracts, then draft their own contracts, interpret a complex contract, followed by team-based rewrites.

LAW 712.description: Negotiation Theory and Application. Develops enhanced negotiation skills and a working understanding of ADR processes and procedures in an interactive classroom experience.

LAW 715.description: ADR Law and Policy: Mediation and Arbitration. Exploration of the origin, development, and practice of mediation, arbitration and other forms of ADR, emphasizing the policies       underlying these increasingly significant and evolving areas.

LAW 718.description: Sports Law in Practice. Sports law is a blend of contract, labor, antitrust, agency, tax, intellectual property, tort, civil rights and constitutional law. Open only to Law Students.

LAW 719.description: Corporate Finance. Legal and economic aspects of corporate finance including capital structure, policy, mergers, takeovers, and freeze-outs; analysis of policy relating to present law and possible reforms.

LAW 726.description: Stereotypes, Prejudice and the Rule of Law. This course examines the role of race (and other markers of social marginality) in the administration of justice in American courts.

LAW 727.description: Partnerships and Limited Liability Companies. This course deals with the formation, features and functions of  general partnerships, limited partnerships and limited liability  companies.  It will also focus on business planning, recognizing  business and legal objectives and selecting the appropriate entity  to accomplish these objectives.

LAW 736.description: Small Business Clinic I. Students provide legal assistance to small businesses, entrepreneurs and non-profit organizations that cannot pay market rates for legal services. Graded CR/NC. Open to Law students only.

LAW 749.description: Securities Regulation. Regulation by state and federal agencies of issuance of, and trading in, stocks, bonds, and other securities. Particular reference to SEC regulations.

LAW 750.description: Federal Indian Law. Introduction to the doctrines of Indian law governing the legal relationship between the United States, states and Indian tribes.

LAW 753.description: Antitrust Law I.  Laws designed to preserve and promote business competition, with heavy emphasis on the federal antitrust laws.

LAW 764.description: International Business Transactions.  Survey of legal aspects of international trade and investment transactions, including tax considerations.

LAW 770.description: Intellectual Property Licensing. Provides students with the foundation for advising clients on Intellectual Property licensing transactions involving patents, software, data and other technology-related rights.

LAW 777.description: Administrative Law and Regulatory Policy. Legal principles subject to judicial control and the alternative   ways in which agencies can be organized to serve their purposes.

LAW 781.description: Externship I. An externship allows a student to gain hands-on legal experience in legal settings. Students will be assigned to a legal services program, government agency, or state or federal judge under faculty supervision. All externships include a classroom component.

LAW 782.description: Externship II. Advanced externship. All externships include a classroom component.

LAW 786.description: Advanced Externships. Advanced externships consist of field work at a placement and a  bi-weekly instructed course. Assignments are designed to support  professional growth as a law student.

LAW 788.description: Racial Ambiguity Blues. Examines the three prevailing concepts of race currently used in the American legal system: biological race, performed race and physical race.

LAW 789.description: Race, Racism and the Law. Understand the reciprocal relationship through which race and racism have shaped American law and how law has shaped popular conceptions of race and racism.

LAW 792.description: Law and Philosophy Seminar. Examination of the best scholarly work currently done by legal, moral and political philosophers.

LAW 796.description: Immigration Clinic II. Continuation of LAW 776. Enrollment restricted to law students. Prerequisite: LAW 776.

LAW 799.description: The Role of the In-House Entertainment Lawyer. Hands-on experience performing legal work on a hypothetical  television program. The class will act as the legal department  under supervision of the department head (instructor).

LAW 801.description: Venture Capital and Emerging Companies. Introduces students to the unique legal and financial aspects of the venture capital industry and the skills needed to represent entrepreneurs and venture capital investors.

LAW 802.description: Human Rights and Climate Change. An examination of the intersection of human rights, environmental  and international law on the obligations of States in connection  with climate change and a survey of international litigation  strategies to address the crisis.

LAW 807.description: Corporate and Commercial Law Seminar. Examine leading legal and economic theories regarding corporate governance.

LAW 808.description: Medical-Legal Community Partnership Practicum. Medical and law students, in conjunction with public policy advocates, work together to identify and improve health outcomes for vulnerable populations.

LAW 809.description: Deposition Strategies and Techniques. Emphasizes strategies and tactics in asking and objecting to questions at a deposition in a civil case. Students will conduct mock depositions.

LAW 815.description: Military Law. A practical introduction to military justice, civil and  operations/international law taught through an interactive  classroom experience by a practicing U.S. Air Force Reserve Judge  Advocate.

LAW 817.description: International Arbitration. Examines methods of dispute resolution used in other countries and compares them to those employed in the United States.

LAW 818.description: Legal Crisis Management. Provides a legal framework for managing crises. Topics covered  include immediate crisis response, internal investigations, legal  holds, governance, fiduciary duties and communication.

LAW 819.description: ADR Ethics. Provides law students, lawyers and professional neutrals with an in-depth examination of the rules guiding our behavior in various dispute resolution processes. Open only to law students.

LAW 820.description: Pretrial Advocacy. Examines conceptual and practical aspects of interviewing,         counseling, negotiation, settlement, drafting and formal advocacy  in the handling of legal cases.

LAW 821.description: Trial Advocacy. Examines decicion-making by counsel in the litigation of cases. Emphasis is given to decisions involving tactics, strategies, and their implications for the functioning of legal institutions and substantive doctrine. Extensive use of simulated trial practice exercises.

lectures.instructor: Caroline Wittcoff; Karen Escalante; Jennifer Chou

LAW 823.description: Corporate Ethics and Compliance. Corporate Compliance, its origins, guiding laws, applicability and  value for companies of all sizes whether large or small, public or  private.

LAW 824.description: Arbitration Advocacy. Helps students understand the basic approaches to preparing and presenting cases in the arbitration context.

LAW 826.description: Employment Dispute Mediation. Provides hands-on experience in mediation of the complex issues of disability, wage and hour, sex and sex harassment, age, race, religion, and national origin.

LAW 827.description: Counseling the Startup Company. Role of the attorney in startup firms: business plan, employment  agreements, lease, stock option plan, financing documents and  distribution and strategic partnership arrangements.  Enrollment  restricted to law students.

LAW 828.description: Mediation Advocacy. Introduces students to the process of mediation, explores the philosophical approaches to mediation and different styles of mediating, develops a working knowledge of the stages of mediation, and cultivates students skills to become effective advocates throughout each stage of the process.

LAW 829.description: Cross-Cultural Dispute Resolution. Brings an international perspective to understanding the impact of culture in the most commonly used international and domestic dispute resolution practices (negotiation, mediation, and arbitration).

LAW 831.description: Feminist Legal Philosophy. Covers feminist philosophy while engaging with contemporary  debates from a variety of perspectives with an emphasis on state  and legal institutions.

LAW 840.description: Global Data Privacy Law and Practice. Introduction to global data privacy law and practices.

LAW 842.description: Partnership Taxation. Explores the fundamentals of federal income taxation of partners and partnerships, including classification, formation, operations, distributions, disposition of partnership interests, partnership terminations and the drafting of partnership agreements.

LAW 843.description: Tax Policy Seminar. Students will write and present papers discussing topics in tax policy.

LAW 845.description: Negotiation Skills. Develops students' negotiating skills through role plays, reflection and instructor feedback.

LAW 848.description: Jurisprudence. Examines questions about the nature of law, the relationship between law and morality and what determines the content of valid law.

LAW 850.description: International Human Rights Clinic II. Continuation of the Inernational Human Rights Clinic

LAW 857.description: Housing Law and Policy Clinic II. Continuation of the Housing Law and Policy Clinic.

LAW 860.description: International Criminal Law. Covers the prosecution, trial and punishment of individuals suspected of crimes considered among the most serious violations of international humanitarian and human rights law.

LAW 864.description: Statutory Torts. Survey of statutorily created causes of action -- covering civil  rights, discrimination, securities, government liability, among  others -- including doctrines such as standing, immunities,  causation and preemption.

LAW 865.description: Legislative Policy Practicum. Provides students with an opportunity to participate in real-world advocacy on juvenile justice issues.

LAW 867.description: Corporate Fraud Seminar. Introduces law students to the real world issues of major civil and criminal corporate fraud.

LAW 869.description: Family Law Mediation Clinic. Teaches the skills and substantive area of the law necessary to successfully mediate cases in the Edelman Children's courthouse in Monterey Park.

LAW 870.description: Legal Writing Fellows. Assist in teaching writing and advocacy. Responsibilities include helping prepare lesson plans and drafting writing assignments and sample answers; leading class exercises; and judging first-year moot court practice rounds. Graded CR/D/F.

LAW 886.description: Intellectual Property Practicum. Providing supervised legal services to USC student films, mastering content clearance, contracts, risk analysis and client counseling within real-world entertainment production.

LAW 887.description: The First Amendment's Religion Clauses:          Religious Liberty                               . Surveys doctrines of the Free Exercise and Establishment Clauses of the First Amendment and related statutory rights through the dual lenses of law and history..

LAW 892.description: Post-Conviction Justice Project II. Continuation of LAW 891. Experiential units.

LAW 893.description: Advanced Clinical Training. For third-year students who wish to continue their clinical  training.

LAW 894.description: Advanced Mediation Clinic. Students learn mediation skills, conduct live mediations and help to run the regular Mediation Clinic.

LAW 896.description: Stigma, Discrimination, and Mental Health Disorders. Examines the stigma against mental illness by and on behalf of the  U.S. government, with special attention to stigma within the  Department of Defense.

LIM 500.description: Foundations of Library and Information Science. History and evolution of libraries and information organizations, including their structure, funding, role in society, and impact on the communities they serve.

LIM 502.description: User-Centered Collection Development. Collection development focused on the needs of patrons, in service of the institutional mission to serve and partner with the broader community.

LIM 503.description: Information Organization and Description for User Engagement. Theories, standards, and tools for the organization and description of information with the goal of equitable and inclusive access for users.

LIM 509.description: Information Sources and Services. Developments in reference and user services, including tools and processes for ethical information evaluation, retrieval and delivery for users in diverse library settings.

LIM 519.description: Leading Values-Driven Information Organizations. Effective application of interdisciplinary, community-centered leadership concepts in libraries and information organizations, with a focus on mission-driven, inclusive strategic planning and change management.

LIM 539.description: Project Management in Information Organizations. Practical applications for leadership and management in library and information organizations, with particular emphasis on project management concepts and methods.

LIM 541.description: Archives and Digital Curation. History and evolution of archival practice, and the strategies and tools needed for contemporary and future-facing archival management, preservation and digital curation.

LIM 549.description: Justice, Equity and Ethics in Information Organizations. History, theory and potential of social justice in library and information organizations, with the goal of implementing services and programs for diverse stakeholders.

LIM 562.description: Transformative Technologies in Library and Information Scien. Role of technology in libraries and information organizations, and potential use and ethical considerations of contemporary and emerging technologies to enhance library services.

LIM 598.description: Capstone in Library and Information Management. Knowledge and skills gained throughout the MMLIS program are synthesized in a culminating capstone project, and deployed in service of career advancement.

LING 107.description: Communication Disorders in Our Communities. Introduction to hearing disorders, motor speech disorders, and pragmatic disorders. The impact of these on effective communication. Common methods of diagnosing and intervening.

LING 115.description: Language and Society. Discourse patterns among diverse social groups in institutional and interpersonal settings; interrelationships among language practices and gender, socioeconomic status, ethnicity; social structures and cultural values as reflected in language policies and practices.

LING 120.description: American Sign Language I. Familiarization with ASL and fingerspelling. Covers visual and gestural communication, comprehension through receptive language skills, basic conversational proficiency, general insights into American Deaf culture.

LING 160.description: Deaf Cultures and Signed Language Communities. Explores Deaf culture and signed language communities as linguistic, social, and cultural groups. Topics include history of signed languages, cultural values, education, and technology.

LING 210.description: Introduction to Linguistics. Empirical study of the sounds and structures of human language;syntax and semantics; language change; linguistic universals.

LING 285.description: Human Language and Technology. Study of human linguistic competence and technologies that simulate it. Phonetics, vibration and signal processing, speech recognition, neural networks.

LING 301.description: Introduction to Phonology and Morphology. A survey of topics in phonology and morphology.

LING 303.description: Introduction to Semantics and Pragmatics. Introduction to meaning in natural language and the methods from logic applied to its study.

LING 385.description: Human Language as Computation. Study of language as a complex natural system that requires elaborate mental computation.

LING 408.description: Sociolinguistics. Language and society: theory and methods in sociolinguistics; dimensions of language variation including gender, identity, class, age, region; personal-level interactions to national-level language policies.

LING 414.description: Morphology. Formal analysis of linguistic data, familiarization with new theoretical models, abstract reasoning in linguistic theory.

LING 433.description: Children's Learning and Cognitive Development. Principles of learning and cognitive development from infancy through adolescence. Prerequisite 336.

LING 465.description: Philosophy of Language.  The nature of communication, meaning, reference, truth,           necessity, speech acts, convention, and language.

LING 485.description: Field Methodology. Elicitation techniques and methodological principles; recording  and analysis of phonological, syntactic and semantic structures;  practical approaches to procedures used in urban and rural  settings.

LING 490.description: Directed Research.  Individual research and readings. Not available for graduate credit.

LING 505C.description: Seminar in Linguistics. Colloquium for presentation and discussion of student research paper.

LING 506.description: Practicum in Phonetics and Phonology. Professional development in phonetics and phonology. Skills workshops, discussion of emerging research in the literature, and internal and external presentations of work in progress.

LING 507.description: Practicum in Syntax and Semantics. Professional development in syntax and semantics. Skills workshops, discussion of emerging research in the literature, and internal and external presentations of work in progress.

LING 508.description: Practicum in Psycholinguistics. Professional development in psycholinguistics. Skills workshops, discussion of emerging research in the literature, and internal and external presentations of work in progress.

LING 531B.description: Phonology.  Traditional views of phonology; generative phonology; current developments in phonological research and theory.

LING 535.description: Syntax and Grammatical Theory. Principles and comparison of modern theories of grammar with special reference to syntax.

LING 536.description: Advanced Semantics. Intensive work in semantic theory, in preparation for a research specialization in the area.

LING 540.description: Field Methods in Linguistics. Recording and analysis of a living language as employed by a native speaker of that language.

LING 579.description: Child Language Development.  Acquisition of grammatical, discourse, and conversational competence; strategies and structures.

LING 580.description: General Phonetics. Familiarization with articulation, transcription, production, and  acoustic analysis of the speech sounds found in the world's  languages.  Also speech technology, perception, and disorders.   Includes laboratory exercises.

LING 585.description: Computational Linguistics. Using hands-on techniques, we study the role of linguistic  knowledge and the procedures that implement it in computational  systems that process natural language.

LING 586.description: Advanced Psycholinguistics.  Current issues in psycholinguistic theory.

LING 590.description: Directed Research.  Research leading to the master's degree. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

LING 594A.description: Master's Thesis. Credit on acceptance of thesis.

LING 594B.description: Master's Thesis. Credit on acceptance of thesis.

LING 595.description: Directed Readings. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department.

LING 602.description: Seminar in Experimental Methods in Linguistics. Topics in quantitataive methods in linguistics research, e.g., covariance structure analysis, multi-dimensional scaling, log linear model, meta-analysis.

LING 632.description: Seminar in Phonetics. Readings in phonetic theory and current research as the framework  for a discussion-oriented class.

LING 790.description: Research.  Research leading to the doctorate. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

LING 794A.description: Doctoral Dissertation.  Credit on acceptance of dissertation. Graded CR/NC.

LING 794B.description: Doctoral Dissertation.  Credit on acceptance of dissertation. Graded CR/NC.

LING 794C.description: Doctoral Dissertation.  Credit on acceptance of dissertation. Graded CR/NC.

MOR 443.description: The Business of Digital Hollywood. An overview of how the media and entertainment (M&E) industries operate. History and changing organizational structures in film, television, music and video games.

MOR 451.description: Mastering Decision Making. Understand the nature, causes, and consequences of deviations from rational choice. Develop frameworks for controlling biases, improving your decision-making, and influencing other peoples decisions.

MOR 452.description: Product Management I - Essentials and Frameworks. Strategic and managerial skills in product management. Frameworks that are essential for managing cross-functional teams, leveraging technology and integrating generative AI for innovation.

MOR 453.description: Product Management II - Execution and Alignment. Utilizing product management frameworks in the execution of key product management responsibilities including team alignment, product prioritization and effective agile development.

MOR 454.description: Applied Product Management and Leadership. Hands-on product management experience via team projects that produce real digital products. Apply product management frameworks in working teams to a real world problem.

MOR 458.description: AI Technology Strategic Management. How to develop strategy approaches for managing new technology in business with a focus on artificial intelligence.

MOR 462.description: Management Consulting. Role of professional consultants; data gathering methods;  consulting approaches from strategy, finance, operations,  information systems, marketing, and human resources; action  planning; ethical and career issues.

MOR 468.description: International Negotiations. Cross-cultural awareness, knowledge, and skills necessary to negotiate effectively with counterparts from other cultures and countries.

MOR 469.description: Negotiation and Persuasion. Theories, strategies, and ethics underlying negotiation and  persuasion in contemporary organizations and societies.   Emphasizes the knowledge and skills needed for effective  negotiation and persuasion.

MOR 473.description: Designing and Leading Teams. Theories and practices for developing and leading teams.  Skills  for creating team structures and facilitating team processes.   Knowledge for diagnosing team problems and devising solutions. Recommended preparation: BUAD 304

MOR 476.description: The Art of Leadership - Leading on a Global Stage. Study of leaders and applied theory to gain an understanding of what is involved in taking public leadership roles on a global level. Open only to students in the USC Warren Bennis Scholars Program.

MOR 478.description: The Art of Leadership - Practical Leadership. Application of leadership skills using goal-setting, self-knowledge and execution opportunities. Open only to students in the USC Warren Bennis Scholars program.

MOR 479.description: The Business of Sports. Addresses the business side of the sports industry; examines  professional sports franchises, amateur athletics, and collegiate  sports and how they relate to corporate America, the media, and  the public sector. Recommended Preparation BUAD 304.

MOR 492.description: Global Strategy. Examination of corporate strategy practices in an international  context.  Effects of cultures, political systems, markets, and  economic systems on developing effective global strategies.

MOR 498.description: Special Topics. Selected topics reflecting current trends and recent developments in organizational behavior, business strategy and organizational theory. (Graded CR/NC)

MOR 499.description: Special Topics. Selected topics reflecting current trends and recent developments in organizational behavior, business strategy and organizational theory.

MOR 530.description: Strategic Leadership in Product Management. Equip students with strategic and managerial skills in product  management, focusing on leading cross-functional teams, leveraging  technology, and integrating generative AI for innovation.

MOR 531.description: Applied Product Management. Hands-on experience managing real products from start to finish.  Essential processes and tools to enhance skills and improve  professional prospects.

MOR 539.description: Timeless Leadership. Examine how historical leaders make decisions via original texts, cases and guest lecturers to develop your own leadership vision.

MOR 543.description: Leading with Mindfulness and Compassion. Explores mindfulness (non-judgmental awareness), compassion and    their relationship to leadership. Focus is on clarity in           productivity using evidence-based cases and direct practice.  Graded CR/NC.

MOR 544.description: Fundamentals of Crisis Management. Types of crises, their developmental stages and nature and the faulty rationalizations that adversely affect businesses. How to recognize, diagnose and prevent crises.

MOR 547.description: Mergers and Acquisitions: Integration and Organization. Organize successful mergers and acquisitions with focus on managing and synthesizing the integration process and impact on people and organizations across functions.

MOR 554.description: Leading Innovation and Change. Practical knowledge on helping organizations develop innovations and lead change to leverage them. Exploration of innovation and change in different organizations and competitive environments.

MOR 555.description: Designing High Performance Organizations. Theory and practice of organization design. How to maximize organization performance by aligning structure, rewards, staffing, processes, and culture with strategy and environment.

MOR 557.description: Strategy and Organization Consulting. How consultants assist clients to formulate strategic plans and realign organizations; approaches used by major consulting firms; information about consulting industry, fee-setting and proposals. Consultant speakers and project.

MOR 564.description: Strategic Innovation: Creating New Markets. How firms in rapidly changing global environments innovate to develop new markets, products and services, delivery systems and organizational processes and competencies.

MOR 565.description: Alliances and Cooperative Strategy. Essential issues and problems of cooperative strategy. Recognize and evaluate collaborative opportunities to develop and assess an overall cooperative strategy. Readings, cases and group project.

MOR 567.description: Interpersonal Influence and Power. Legitimate and effective use of power to resolve conflicts and mobilize action through understanding the talent and self-interest of people involved in decision-making. Readings, cases.

MOR 569.description: Negotiation and Deal-Making. Strategies and dynamics of deal-making; practical skills necessary to win in a range of business transactions conducted in domestic and international settings. Cases, role-playing, films and simulations.

MOR 570.description: Leading Effective Teams. Analytical and behavioral tools that will enable students to effectively diagnose complex work group dynamics and take action to improve group performance.

MOR 571.description: Leadership and Executive Development. Contemporary approaches to leadership, including corporate practices to develop leaders; examples of successful and derailed executives. Students self-assess personal leadership and draft development plans. Readings, speakers, cases.

MOR 574A.description: Leading and Coaching: Foundations and Practicum. Marshall MBA Leadership Fellows Program (MLFP). Learn, practice and teach leadership. Engage in critical thinking and problem solving. (a) Foundations. (b) Practicum. Application required.

MOR 579.description: The Business of Sports Entertainment. Business practices and issues in different sports markets including growth opportunities and innovative marketing strategies for attracting and retaining fans and corporate sponsors. Industry speakers.

MOR 588.description: Corporate Strategy and Competitive Dynamics. Central challenges facing executives in multi-business firms; toolkit for analyzing and executing strategic and operational aspects of corporate advantage, M&As; and competitive dynamics.

MOR 590.description: Directed Research. Research leading to the master's degree.  Maximum units which may  be applied to the degree to be determined by the department.   Graded CR/NC.

MOR 592.description: Field Research in Management and Organization. Individual or team projects studying the management practices of an industry, company, government agency, country geographic region, etc. Proposal, data collection, analyses, and written report. Graded CR/NC.

MOR 593.description: Independent Research in Management and Organization. Independent research beyond normal course offerings. Proposal, research and written report/paper required. Graded CR/NC.

MOR 595.description: Internship in Management and Organization. Supervised on-the-job business experience in the student's area of interest. (Curricular Practical Training.)

MOR 596.description: Research Practicum in Management and Organization. Hands-on practical experience working with a Marshall faculty member in the Management and Organization Department on an ongoing research project. Graded CR/NC.

MOR 597.description: Consulting Project in Management and Organization. Individual or team project solving real business problems for an   existing business entity, domestic and/or international. Proposal, field research, analyses and oral and written  presentations. Graded CR/NC.

MOR 599.description: Special Topics. Selected topics reflecting current trends and recent developments in management and policy sciences. May be repeated only if topic is different.

MOR 602.description: Seminar in Organization Theory. Survey of organization theory with focus on the history and development of research on organizations.

MOR 605.description: Research Methods in Organizational Behavior. Design and analysis of behavioral research; methods may include experiments, survey research, qualitative research, statistical analysis, special topics. Emphasis on rigor, validity and statistical power.

MOR 790.description: Research. Research leading to the doctorate. Open only to Marshall Ph.D. students specializing in Management and Organization. Graded CR/NC.

MKT 402.description: Introduction to Marketing Analytics. Analyze marketing data and develop actionable insights to guide marketing decisions. Apply statistical tools, machine learning, and economic analysis to digital marketing problems.

MKT 405.description: Marketing Communication and Promotion Strategy. Develop skills for effective marketing communication and promotion. Consider objectives and components of a strategic plan (including marketplace analysis, research, campaign development, and media planning).

MKT 410.description: Professional Selling. Principles of business-to-business selling and its function in marketing strategy and the marketing mix. Explore professional selling as a career option.

MKT 425.description: Digital Marketing Fundamentals. Examine the changing world of the connected consumer. Gain introductory knowledge about consumers online and digital marketing tactics across industries.

MKT 428.description: Social Media Strategy for Business. Examine the use of social media for business across industries. Understand theories and frameworks for strategic content creation and posting as technology and platforms evolve.

MKT 445.description: New Product Development and Branding. Learn how marketers create new brands, products and services. Discuss and examine creative ideation, research and development, brand image management and legal issues in branding.

MKT 450.description: Consumer Behavior and Marketing. Examine diverse consumers behavior including acquisition, usage and disposition of products. Understand the psychological, social and cultural influences that drive consumers decisions.

MKT 451.description: User Experience (UX) and Design for Marketing. Theories and frameworks to enhance customer engagement and  satisfaction by integrating UX principles into design and  marketing strategies.

MKT 461.description: Marketing in the Entertainment Industry. Examine the marketing of products and brands in the entertainment industry (including movies, TV shows, music and video games).

MKT 465.description: Multicultural Marketing. Examine how marketers adapt the marketing mix to serve consumers from diverse cultures, considering differing social norms and regulations across the global marketplace.

MKT 467.description: Marketing in the Gaming Industry. Examine issues traditionally crucial to the marketing of games including launch marketing, consumer insights, brand management, data analytics, performance marketing and community engagement.

MKT 479.description: Sports Marketing. Examine the marketing mix (i.e., product, price, place and promotion) across the global sports industry, including leagues, teams, athletes, events and apparel and equipment companies.

MKT 486.description: Fashion, Luxury and Lifestyle Marketing: A  Global Perspective. Fundamentals of fashion, luxury and lifestyle marketing in a  global market including visiting relevant companies in Italy  during spring recess.

MKT 512.description: Customer Insights and Analysis. Use of marketing research techniques and technologies such as databases and statistical tools to collect, analyze and act upon customer information.

MKT 525.description: Consumer Behavior. Analyze theories of consumer behavior and their relevance to the modern marketplace; examine psychological, social, and cultural factors influencing consumers across contexts.

MKT 526.description: Advertising and Social Media: Strategy and Analytics. Effective advertising in an era of social media including strategy and analytics for crafting ad messages, testing ads, budgeting and media scheduling.

MKT 530.description: New Product Development. Systematic approach to product development and management; processes, techniques, and concepts firms use to develop, test, and introduce products and to manage products over their lifecycle.

MKT 533.description: Brand Strategy and Management. Analyze the behavioral foundations of brands and brand development; explore various marketing tools and tactics for brand development and management.

MKT 551.description: From Strategy to Execution: User Experience (UX) and Design. Explores the dynamic relationship between user experience (UX) and marketing strategy. Students utilize UX design principles to address product and marketing challenges.

MKT 556.description: Digital Marketing Strategy. Develop strategy for digital marketing using existing and emerging tools and technologies; analyze various tactics, including search, display, video, social media, e-commerce, and influencers.

MKT 560.description: Marketing Strategy. Design and implementation of marketing strategies applied to domestic and global business challenges that span multiple industries complimented by a consumer packaged goods marketing strategic plan project.

MKT 566.description: Decision Making Using Marketing Analytics. Applications and models of marketing-related data analyses to the development of data-driven marketing strategies and making data-driven marketing decisions.

MKT 567.description: Marketing Metrics for Business Decisions. Application, development, interpretation and implementation (in Excel and Tableau) of marketing metrics using case studies, data, and practitioner talks.

MKT 568.description: Geographic Information Systems Applications in Marketing. Fundamentals of geographic information systems; location analytics and spatial thinking as they relate to data-driven decision-making in marketing strategy and tactics.

MKT 586.description: Fashion, Luxury and Lifestyle Marketing. Examination of marketing issues and challenges within a variety of business settings in the fashion, luxury goods and lifestyle sectors in the global marketplace.

MKT 590.description: Directed Research. Research leading to the master's degree.  Maximum units which may  be applied to the degree to be determined by the department.   Graded CR/NC.

MKT 592.description: Field Research in Marketing. Individual or team projects studying the marketing practices of an industry, company, government agency, country, geographic region, etc. Proposal, data collection, analyses, and written report. Graded CR/NC.

MKT 593.description: Independent Research in Marketing. Independent research beyond normal course offerings. Proposal, research and written report/paper required. Graded CR/NC.

MKT 595.description: Internship in Marketing. Supervised on-the-job business experience in the field of marketing. (Curricular Practical Training.) Graded CR/NC.

MKT 597.description: Consulting Project in Marketing. Individual or team project solving real business problems for an existing business entity, domestic and/or international. Proposal, field research, analyses and oral and written presentations. Graded CR/NC

MKT 599.description: Special Topics. Current trends, recent developments, and emerging topics in the field of Marketing. Topics vary each semester. May be repeated only if topic is different.

MKT 616.description: Consumer Behavior Theory and Research. Behavioral research and theory on consumer behavior with a focus on emotions, categorization, knowledge, inferences, attitudes, social influences and environmental influences on buying and consumption.

MKT 620.description: Advanced Quantitative Models in Marketing. Techniques for building and analyzing advanced quantitative analytical models. Develop and estimate various state-of-the-art models of consumer choice and firm decisions. Open only to Doctoral students.

MKT 621.description: Research Forum. Seminar. Review and discuss current research in Marketing. Presentations by faculty, visiting researchers, and advanced students. Open to Marshall Ph.D. students only. Graded CR/NC.
