PSYC 594B.description: Master's Thesis. Credit on acceptance of Thesis. Graded CR/NC.

PSYC 594Z.description: Master's Thesis. Credit on acceptance of Thesis. Graded CR/NC.

PSYC 595.description: Practicum in Clinical Psychology. Supervised experience in interviewing skills and in assessment, including psychological test administration, and the preparation of reports. Graded CR/NC.

PSYC 597.description: Internship for Curricular Practical Training. Part-time or full-time, practical work experience in the students field of study. The internship must be located at an off-campus facility. Students are individually supervised by faculty. May not be taken until the student has completed at least two semesters of enrollment in the graduate program.

PSYC 599.description: Special Topics. Selected topics in the various specialty areas within psychology at the graduate level. Topic will vary from semester to semester.

PSYC 612.description: Seminar in Advanced Social Psychology. An intensive consideration of selected concepts, theories, and research problems in social psychology.

PSYC 619.description: Psychological Intervention. Study of clinical psychological treatment: Research and theory     about major psychological approaches to intervention. (One of 4    clinical psychology core courses: PSYC 514, PSYC 515, PSYC 619,  PSYC 620.)

PSYC 627.description: Machine Cognition. Explores Machine Cognition, tracing AI's history from symbolic systems to LLMs, analyzing emergent capabilities and the philosophical questions of artificial minds.

PSYC 691B.description: Internship in Clinical Psychology.  Supervised clinical work in an approved mental health setting. Graded CR/NC. Prerequisite: Good standing in clinical program and departmental approval.

PSYC 695.description: Advanced Practicum in Clinical Psychology. Didactic practicum combining theory and research on psychological intervention with clinical practice in assessment and treatment, focused on particular client groups or disorders. Graded CR/NC.

PSYC 696.description: Externship for Practical Training. Externship for Practical Training is for clinical-related training experience in the students fieldof study. Students are individually supervised at their site.

PSYC 790.description: Research.  Research leading to the doctorate. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

PSYC 794A.description: Doctoral Dissertation. Credit on acceptance of Dissertation. Graded IP/CR/NC.

PSYC 794B.description: Doctoral Dissertation. Credit on acceptance of Dissertation. Graded IP/CR/NC.

PSYC 794C.description: Doctoral Dissertation.  Credit on acceptance of Dissertation. Graded IP/CR/NC.

PSYC 794D.description: Doctoral Dissertation.  Credit on acceptance of Dissertation. Graded IP/CR/NC.

PSYC 794Z.description: Doctoral Dissertation. Credit on acceptance of Dissertation. Graded IP/CR/NC.

PUBD 512.description: Cultural Diplomacy. Provides overview of formal cultural diplomacy and concentrates on  ways in which non-governmental entities communicate across  international boundaries and the effects of those interchanges.

PUBD 520.description: Regional Studies in Public Diplomacy. In-depth examination of historical, political, economic, cultural  factors that influence public diplomacy efforts within specific  geographic regions.

PUBD 526.description: Public Diplomacy Evaluation. Critical examination of challenges and benefits of measuring Public Diplomacy's impact; terminology and mechanics of evaluation, the measurement community, and varying approaches for evaluation

PUBD 590.description: Directed Research. Research leading to the master's degree.  Maximum units which may  be applied to the degree to be determined by the school.  Graded  CR/NC.

PUBD 596.description: Practicum in Public Diplomacy Research         . Development and production of original research-based project in  the area of public diplomacy.  Graded CR/NC.

PR 209.description: Effective Writing for Strategic Public Relations and Adverti. Focus on the unique writing requirements of social, online, broadcast, print and other media in public relations/advertising; emphasis on judgment, context and audience understanding. Non-majors who are interested in enrolling must have at least a 2.5 GPA.

PR 250.description: Strategic Public Relations and Advertising: An Introduction. Strategies/practices in the growing field of public relations and advertising, including landmark cases, campaign planning; special emphasis on historical roots, current and future practice.

PR 340.description: Introduction to Advertising. History and development of advertising; basic advertising campaigns showing relationships of marketing, creative, print and electronic media.

PR 351A.description: Multichannel Strategy and Content Creation. Introduction to media relations, social media and influencer engagement; intensive writing and creating multimedia content for traditional, emerging and social media.

PR 352.description: Public Relations Media and Content for Non-Majors. Learn advanced public relations writing and editing, basic design skills and sophisticated video planning, shooting, editing and production skills.

PR 400.description: Practicum for PR Media Center. A hands-on learning lab, exploring how to create original social media content while adhering to media production cycle.

PR 410.description: London Calling: Public Relations in the UK Hub. Examines how politics affects and influences public relations campaigns in the UK and Europe.

PR 427.description: Structured Inquiry in Public Relations and Advertising. Apply contemporary research methods to create actionable insights for integrated, multi-channel communication campaigns, including social media monitoring, measurement and evaluation.

PR 429.description: Business and Economic Foundations of Public Relations and Ad. Relationship between public relations/advertising and other organizational disciplines; understanding business goals and objectives; economic literacy; financial/investor relations; how PR/communication agencies are built and managed.

PR 431.description: Integrated Media Planning and Buying. Fundamentals of media planning and buying across traditional and new media; how each media channel works independently and as part of an integrated media plan.

PR 434.description: Advertising Campaign Construction. Develop an integrated marketing communication campaign that will compete against other universities in the national Collegiate Effie competition.

PR 435.description: Advertising Copywriting. Master the art of advertising copywriting. Develop breakthrough concepts and craft compelling campaigns across all media channels. Transform creativity into strategic impact.

PR 450.description: Building Integrated Campaigns. In-depth study of methods for planning, managing and evaluating strategic communication campaigns; critical analysis of contemporary cases; development of campaigns for real world clients.

PR 452.description: Public Relations in Entertainment. Public relations in the design, promotion, and presentation of popular entertainment, including films, broadcasting, music, expositions, amusement parks, resorts and arenas.

PR 454.description: Sports Public Relations. Introduction to the field of sports information and promotion, including lectures, media assignments, role-playing, and presentations by sports professionals.

PR 457.description: The Role of Celebrity in Public Relations. Understanding of the history and application of celebrity in public relations, focusing on the entertainment industry and the notoriety attached to politics and the media.

PR 458.description: Political Public Relations and Advocacy. Application of public relations principles to the context of political campaigns; emphasis on message development and delivery; relationship between candidate, news media, and electorate.

PR 464.description: Advanced Lifestyle Public Relations. In-depth look at various aspects of Lifestyle PR with special emphasis on food, fashion and beauty, travel/tourism, hospitality, furniture/housewares, toys and more.

PR 478.description: Social Media Analytics: Data, Content Creation and Campaign . Application of monitoring tools to become social media analysts and real-time content creators; interpretation of large data sets drawn from the social web; understanding of how to present data visually for optimal impact.

PR 486.description: Multimedia PR Content: Introduction to Digital Design Tools. Hands-on lab; producing multimedia content; basic principles of design; tools and techniques to create digital images and layouts.

PR 487.description: Multimedia PR Content: Introduction to Audio/Video Tools. Hands-on lab; audio/video tools for conceiving, shooting, editing, delivering and archiving compelling stories for online audiences; personal brand building; digital storytelling trends and applications.

PR 490.description: Directed Research. Individual research and readings. Not available for graduate credit.

PR 491.description: Fan Relations. Examines fan relationships and explores fan activation strategies across sports, television, motion pictures, music, comic books, theme parks, social media and more.

PR 492.description: Personal Branding. Learn to build, promote and manage a personal brand through critical analysis, case study, interactive interpretation and creative problem solving.

PR 498.description: Public Relations Honors Seminar. Leadership workshop inspires students to be braver and more creative; encourages them to discover their leadership potential/explore new challenges inside and outside of classroom.

PR 499.description: Special Topics. Selected topics in public relations.

PR 501.description: Public Policy Communication. Study and evaluation of communications campaigns by civil society actors to influence public policy with a focus on messaging and efforts to shape news coverage.

PR 523.description: Advanced Audience Insight Mining. Provides student training with cutting-edge digital research methods and applied data analytic skills relevant to current and future public relations and advertising practices.

PR 524.description: Multimedia Content Creation for Brand Storytelling I. Covers the conceptualization and creation of strategy-based, engaging, primarily web-based multimedia content for use by organizations of all types.

PR 529.description: Business and Economic Foundations for Communicators. Speaking the language of the board room; understanding business goals and objectives; economic literacy; financial/investor relations;  understanding organizational disciplines and how they relate to corporate communication; PR/communication business processes and management.

PR 565.description: Corporate Public Relations and Reputation. Learn all aspects of corporate communications and reputation management through real-time news analysis, cases and senior guest speakers from the world's largest, most admired companies.

PR 568.description: Crisis Management in Strategic Public Relations. Focuses on theories, concepts and practices in risk assessment, issues monitoring, and crisis anticipation/management in a wide variety of organizational contexts, and from multiple perspectives.

PR 590.description: Directed Research. Research leading to the master's degree. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department.

PR 598.description: Improvisational Leadership. Leadership workshop inspires stepping outside of comfort zones to be braver and more creative.  Encourages discovery of leadership potential by exploring new ideas and challenges.

PRSM 500.description: Strategic Planning for Multichannel Communication Campaigns. Explores the contemporary practices of branding, advertising and public relations, and their expanding role in the development of multichannel communication campaign plans.

PRSM 505.description: Data-Driven Brand Storytelling. Explores the evaluation of research and analysis methods, generating data insights and creating compelling and accurate stories using data visualization techniques.

PRSM 510.description: Leadership and Ethics for Communication Practitioners. Explores the leadership skills and ethics required in todays complex organizations, communication with key stakeholders, creative problem solving and promoting diversity, equity, inclusion and access.

PRSM 515.description: Business and Economic Literacy for Communicators. Covers fundamental business, finance and economics knowledge needed to better align the communication function with organizational goals and communicate effectively with key stakeholders.

PRSM 520.description: Multiplatform Content Creation I. Introduces brand storytelling through the creation of content across multiple channels and platforms using applicable tools, focusing on design and layout.

PRSM 525.description: Multiplatform Content Creation II. Covers brand storytelling through the creation of content across multiple channels and platforms using applicable tools, with a focus on image, audio and video elements.

PRSM 530.description: Employee Communication. Explores employee communication strategies, tools and channels used to engage employees and develop them as brand advocates in support of organizational purpose and goals.

PRSM 535.description: Social Media Advertising. Covers the development of comprehensive social media advertising strategies that maximize budgets, ethically target their audiences and meet the goals of communication campaigns.

PRSM 540.description: Influencer Relationship Management. Explores how influence works, influencer-related functions in public relations, marketing, brand management and advertising, managing influencers and ethical considerations in influencer campaigns.

PRSM 545.description: Crisis Communication. Explores crises, their potential impacts and ethical considerations and the role of communication practitioners in crafting strategic messaging and developing comprehensive crisis communication plans.

PRSM 550.description: Brand Purpose Communication. Explores best practices for brand communication, social issue engagement and advocacy, value alignment, guiding stakeholders on purpose communication and planning purpose-led campaigns or projects.

PRSM 555.description: Emerging Game-Changers for Communication Practitioners. Explores impacts of emerging technologies, innovation and organizational culture concepts and the centrality of emerging technologies in shaping the digital future.

QBIO 105.description: Introduction to Quantitative Biology Seminar. Introduction to quantitative biology and its role in biology and relationship to chemistry, computer science, engineering, mathematics, medicine and physics, including the field's impact on industry.

QBIO 110.description: Drug Discovery: From Genes to Medicines. The course will explore the science of modern drug discovery and development, its key challenges and pitfalls in the personal health and socioeconomic context.

QBIO 305.description: Statistics for Biological Sciences. Statistical methods in biological science and medicine, including populations and samples, random sampling, confidence intervals, paired samples and regression.

QBIO 310.description: Statistical Thinking for Quantitative Biology. Introduction to statistical theory with higher-level mathematics for biological data analysis. Programming in R. Discussion of techniques to describe, visualize and model different data types.

QBIO 465.description: Artificial Intelligence in Biology and Medicine. AI techniques including traditional machine learning and advanced deep learning methods for genomics, system biology, data integration, drug discovery and medical imaging; project-based.

QBIO 478.description: Computational Genome Analysis. Introduction to algorithms and statistics for genome analysis and their applications. Analysis of DNA sequencing, sequence comparison, genetic variation, gene expression, disease association and evolution.

QBIO 490.description: Directed Research. Individual research and readings. Project approval by  faculty adviser and QCB department required.

QBIO 494.description: Quantitative Biology Honors Thesis. Experience in conducting research and writing an honors thesis or publishable manuscript under the supervision of a faculty adviser.

QBIO 502.description: Molecular Biology for Quantitative Scientists. An in-depth study of molecular biology techniques and experiments emphasizing those that can generate big data. Intended for quantitative science and engineering students.

QBIO 542.description: Seminar in Computational Biology. Experience and training in giving science research presentations. Students will discuss recent research in computational biology and bioinformatics.

QBIO 555.description: Scientific Writing in Quantitative and Computational Biology. Practical guidance on the writing of scientific articles and research proposals in the field of Quantitative and Computational Biology.

QBIO 565.description: Artificial Intelligence in Computational Biology. Deep learning and artificial intelligence methods for genomics, transcriptomics, structural and systems biology, drug design, biological imaging including classical and emerging architectures, and research applications.

QBIO 578A.description: Computational Molecular Biology. Algorithms and data structures for genomic sequences: linear time text matching, Burrows-Wheeler transform, assembly and alignment, dynamic programming, RNA secondary structure and tree construction.

QBIO 578B.description: Computational Molecular Biology. Applications of mathematical, statistical and computational methods to data from molecular biology: significance of alignment scores, hidden Markov models, evolution and gene expression analysis.

QBIO 590.description: Directed Research. Research leading to a graduate degree. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

QBIO 596.description: Internship for Curricular Practical Training. Part-time or full-time, practical work experience in the student's field of study. The internship must be located at an off-campus facility. Students are supervised by faculty. May not be taken until the student has completed one semester of enrollment in a graduate program with a cumulative 3.0 GPA. The course is graded CR/NC.

QBIO 790.description: Research. Research leading to the doctorate. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

QBIO 794A.description: Doctoral Dissertation. For doctoral students who have passed the qualifying exam. Credit on acceptance of dissertation.

QBIO 794B.description: Doctoral Dissertation. For doctoral students who have passed the qualifying exam. Credit on acceptance of dissertation.

QBIO 794C.description: Doctoral Dissertation. For doctoral students who have passed the qualifying exam. Credit on acceptance of dissertation.

QBIO 794D.description: Doctoral Dissertation. For doctoral students who have passed the qualifying exam. Credit on acceptance of dissertation.

QBIO 794Z.description: Doctoral Dissertation. For doctoral students who have passed the qualifying exam. Credit on acceptance of dissertation.

RED 200.description: Introduction to Real Estate. Basic understanding of the real estate industry, the process of real estate development and investment, and the key players involved.

RED 201.description: Real Estate Career Seminar. Career assessment and preparation; real estate industry overview; reflection on experiences.

RED 301.description: Real Estate Internship Seminar. Real estate development skills for practice; internship seminar; leadership, group dynamics and presentation skills; application of management; organizational diversity; reflection on experiences.

RED 325.description: Introduction to Finance in Cities. Basic understanding of public finance, public debt, public-private joint ventures, time value of money, present value, risk and return, discounted cash flows, leverage and taxes.

RED 362.description: Real Estate Development Fundamentals. Real estate overview; evolution of cities and neighborhoods; product types; introduction to valuation.

RED 375.description: Real Estate Development Analysis. Real estate development feasibility and analysis; underwriting local fundamentals including neighborhood and city change, real estate capital flows.

RED 398.description: Shaping Cities Through Real Estate. Cities and urban form created through various real estate product types. Case studies and site visits.

RED 417.description: History of Planning and Development. Historical evolution of planning and development. How changing modes of planning and development have shaped the built landscape throughout the century.

RED 425.description: Designing Livable Communities. Theories and concepts of livable communities and good city form; case studies of historical and current best practices; field visits; collaborative design project.

RED 435.description: Analyzing Real Estate Markets. Macro and micro-analysis of urban property markets; demographics; location choice; regulation.

RED 437.description: Advanced Finance and Investment for Real Estate  Development                                     . Advanced real estate principles. Underwriting property valuation and deal structure including risk and return. Debt and equity markets; difference between development and existing assets.

RED 490.description: Directed Research. Individual research and readings.

RED 510.description: Real Estate Practice and Principles. Fundamental principles of real estate analysis; economics; capital markets; development decision making; relationships between real estate markets and federal, state and local government policies; property value.

RED 512.description: Real Estate Project Analysis. Fundamental economic theories; analytical techniques; practical applications for market analysis of various forms of real estate.

RED 546.description: Applications of Real Estate Finance to Problems of Developme. Advanced topics in finance applied to cases and problems of real estate development; emphasis on structuring, finance and evaluation of various types of development projects.

RED 562.description: Legal Issues in Real Estate Development. Ownership and transfer of real estate; formation and enforcement  of contracts; business associations; environmental regulation;  taxation of property transfers; acquiring, financing, leasing of  commercial property.

RED 575.description: Community Design and Site Planning. Physical implementation of development projects. Students will develop concept plan, preliminary design and marketing plan for selected domestic and/or international development sites.

RED 585.description: Comparative International Development Workshop. Comparative study tour focused on understanding international real  estate development practices and markets, site visits and meeting  with principals.

RED 598.description: Real Estate Product Development. An evaluation of various real estate development product types. Case studies and site visits.

RNR 050.description: International Academy Holding Course . Course created per request from the International Academy to  create a zero unit, zero charge course for the purpose of enabling  services for the student  population.  Tuition is paid directly to  the Academy.

RNR 051.description: International Academy Holding Course (Part II). Course created per request from the International Academy to  create a zero unit, zero charge course for the purpose of enabling  services for the student population. This course serves the  popuation that has successfully completed RNR-050.  Tuition is  paid directly to the Academy.

RSCI 508.description: Quality Assurance for Drugs and Biologics. Design and implementation of a quality system assuring the quality and safety of pharmaceuticals and biologics, according to relevant FDA and international regulations and guidance documents.

RSCI 509.description: Quality Assurance, Medical Devices and Combination Products. Design of systems according to FDA and international regulations and guidelines to ensure the quality and safety of medical devices and combination products.

RSCI 511.description: Introduction to Medical Product Regulation. Introduction to regulatory environments surrounding medical product development, manufacturing and marketing; operation of federal, state and international regulatory bodies.

RSCI 513.description: Regulation of Medical Devices and Diagnostics. Development and testing of new medical products according to U.S. and international regulatory requirements.

RSCI 519.description: Global Regulation of Medical Products. Regulatory requirements governing medical products in European Union, Asia and other global markets.

RSCI 520.description: Introduction to Risk Management for Health Care  Providers                                       . Historical development, formal language and theoretical approaches  to risk management in health care and medical product environment;  policies, regulations, standards; liability prevention and loss  control.  Recommended preparation: undergraduate degree in  pharmacy, medical or independent health sciences, engineering or  equivalent mix of post-secondary training and industry  experience.  (Duplicates credit in MPTX 520.)  Recommended  preparation: undergraduate degree in pharmacy, medical or  independent health sciences, engineering or equivalent mix of  post-secondary training and industry experience, enrollment in  M.S., Regulatory Science.

RSCI 521.description: Seminars in Regulatory Science. Current problems in regulatory affairs, legal management, preclinical and clinical testing, scientific evaluation and quality assurance. (Duplicates credit in former MPTX 521.) Graded CR/NC. Recommended preparation: undergraduate degree in pharmacy, medical or independent health sciences, engineering or equivalent mix of post secondary training and industry experience; enrollment in MS Regulatory Science program.

RSCI 522.description: Introduction to Clinical Trial Design and Statistics. Clinical designs and statistics commonly used to test medical products in general populations and special patient groups.

RSCI 537.description: Clinical Trial Project Management. Clinical Trials management and operations are vital aspects in the design, planning, conduct and reporting of successful research projects and portfolios.

RSCI 541.description: Drug Development, Reimbursement, and Marketing. Survey of drug development strategies; health economics and outcomes researches and reimbursements; emphasis on coverage determination process and FDA and CMS parallel review process

RSCI 542.description: Validation Processes and Principles. Explore how regulated industries, such as medical product manufacturing use validation to ensure compliant, consistent, and high-quality products by integrating science, business and project management principles.

RSCI 590.description: Directed Research. Research leading to the master's degree. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

RSCI 601.description: Biomedical Commerce. Introduction to business principles appropriate to medical  products, including: supply and demand, product entry-exit  strategies, financing, reimbursement, marketing and pricing in  global marketplace.  Recommended preparation: undergraduate degree  in pharmacy, medical or independent health sciences, engineering  or equivalent mix of post-secondary training and industry  experience; enrollment in M.S., Regulatory Science.

RSCI 603.description: Managing Complex Projects. Theory and methods to manage complex projects in medical products  sectors; timelines, intellectual property, security, contracts,  budgets, review activities, reports, electronic tools,  cross-cultural communication.  Recommended Preparation:  Undergraduate or professional degree in pharmacy, medical or  independent health sciences, engineering or equivalent mix of  post-secondary training and industry experience.

RSCI 630.description: Directed Field-Research Project. Research/policy analysis conducted under preceptor supervision in an industrial or governmental setting.

REL 111.description: The World of the Hebrew Bible. The Hebrew Bible in the cultural setting of the ancient Near East; the formation of theological and ethical concepts which have shaped Western culture.

REL 112.description: Religions of Ancient Egypt and the Near East. Religions, cultures, and values of ancient Egypt and Near East (Iran, Iraq, Israel, Syria, Lebanon, Arabia, Turkey) and their legacies in contemporary society.

REL 125.description: Introduction to Christianity: Antiquity to 1500. Survey of the changing beliefs and practices of the Christian religion from its origins through early modernity (100 CE - 1500 CE), with special attention to different varieties of Christian literature.

REL 132.description: Origins of Western Religions. Examination of Judaism, Christianity, and Islam in their origins and their development in relation to Western civilization.

REL 134.description: Introduction to Buddhism. Focus primarily on works of Buddhist literature written in a       variety of genres.  Introduction of basic teachings that link      Buddhist traditions across time and space.

REL 141.description: Global Religions in Los Angeles. Congregational and individual expressions of religion in Los Angeles.

REL 315.description: Thought and Life of Islam.  History, thought, institutions, and religious practices of Islam.

REL 340.description: Introduction to Indian Philosophy. An introduction to Indian philosophy, including major schools of thought in Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain philosophies. No previous knowledge of Indian religions or philosophy required.

REL 350.description: Drugs, Alcohol, Visions and Altered States in Religion. Examines the history and meaning of drugs, alcohol and altered states of mind in world religions across history.

REL 468.description: Sociology of Religion. The role of religion in modern society from the standpoint of sociological theory and research.

REL 490.description: Directed Research.  Individual research and readings. Not available for graduate credit.

REL 491.description: Undergraduate Honors Research. Individual research for honors in the major leading to a  substantial project.

REL 625.description: Advanced Graduate Seminar in Global Islam. Exploration of themes and traditions of Islam as they appear globally in a variety of specific country contexts.

REL 701.description: Research Seminar in Religious Studies. Skills for academic professionalization, presentation of research in progress and formal responses to academic writing.

RISK 380.description: Introduction to Enterprise Risk Management. Understand the concept of risk, risk assessment, and management frameworks. Learn to identify, analyze, manage and mitigate, and communicate this risk to stakeholders. Duplicates credit in the former ACCT 380.

RISK 385.description: Introduction to Risk Management and Insurance. Understand the underlying economics, structure, and business models of an organization (often an insurance carrier) willing to accept risk for diverse situations: property, life, healthcare. Duplicates credit in the former ACCT 385.

RISK 386.description: Managing Risks and Crises in Media, Hospitality and Tech. Examination of risks in the media, hospitality and tech industries  and the ways to prepare, manage and recover from crisis  situations.

RISK 387.description: Risk Management in Entertainment, Sports and the Arts. Knowledge and skills needed to identify, analyze, control, finance and report on the risks particular to entertainment, sports and the arts. Duplicates credit in the former ACCT 387.

RISK 388.description: Innovating Risk Solutions in Disruptive Environments. Develop the skills needed to think critically about identified and assessed risks and develop innovative solutions to control and transfer those risks. Duplicates credit in the former ACCT 388.

RISK 580.description: Advanced Enterprise Risk Management. The practical application of enterprise risk management across a broad spectrum of business settings and industry types, from start-up to multinational organizations.

RISK 583.description: The Top Five Risks and What to Do About Them. Examination of what boards and management at large and midsize companies think are the top five risks in business.

RISK 599.description: Special Topics. Current developments in the field of Risk Management. Topics vary from semester to semester. May be repeated only if topic is different.

RUSS 120.description: Beginning Russian I. Introduction to the Russian language with emphasis on basic conversational skills, major points of grammar and reading.

RUSS 140.description: Russian Language and Culture in the Post-Soviet Space. Immersive introduction to Russian language and culture, covering Cyrillic, basic grammar,communication and cultural insights into the post-Soviet world.

RUSS 150.description: Beginning Russian II. Continuation of RUSS 120.

RUSS 220.description: Intermediate Russian I. Development of thematic conversational skills with emphasis on extended dialogue. Review of basic morphology with special attention to verbs of motion. Reading of authentic material is emphasized.

RUSS 250.description: Intermediate Russian II. Continuation of RUSS 220. Development of proficiency in conversation skills, reading and writing.

RUSS 340.description: Intercultural Communication in Russian. Advanced language training focusing on specific issues of communication with Russians. Analysis and translation of literary texts. Advanced syntax. Conducted in Russian.

RUSS 500.description: Topics in Advanced Russian. Study of Russian required for graduate work and professional activities.

SCOR 403.description: Introduction to Scoring Movies and Television. Practical composition course covering the unique art, craft, and technology involved in writing and integrating music for animated and live-action visual media.

SCOR 405.description: Introduction to Scoring Video Games. Practical composition course covering the unique art, craft, and technology involved in composing and integrating video-game music.

SCOR 490.description: Directed Research. Individual research and readings. Not available for graduate credit.

SCOR 501.description: Individual Instruction. Secondary instruction for graduate music majors or instruction for graduate non-music majors.

SCOR 502.description: Individual Instruction in Advanced Screen Scoring. Individual instruction and review of students work. Selected composers, orchestrators, filmmakers, and other important industry collaborators offer their insights on scoring and career building.

SCOR 503B.description: Advanced Scoring for Motion Pictures and Television. Scoring principles involved in designing, timing, and composing scores for video projects, including documentaries, animated, and live-action projects. Will also include composing for live recording sessions.

SCOR 504B.description: Orchestral Scoring. Explores the sounds of and notations for the major orchestral instruments; provides instruction on implementation of those instruments in scoring and orchestrating for the screen.

SCOR 505B.description: Advanced Game Scoring and Integration. Explores more sophisticated principles and techniques involved in the unique aspects of composing and integrating music for video games.

SCOR 509.description: Music Editing and Spotting for Media Productions. Processes and techniques used for the planning and workflow of a score within a media production.

SCOR 511B.description: History of Film Scoring. Examines the evolution of movie music from 1920s to present. Includes recorded interviews with the most significant film composers and film clips of their work.

SCOR 512.description: Entrepreneurialism for the Screen Composer. Addresses challenges facing emerging screen composers, including negotiating deals; establishing a studio, production budgets, and a publishing business; tracking royalties; licensing music; and engaging representation.

SCOR 521B.description: Recording, Mixing and Editing for the Screen Composer. Addresses the need for modern-day screen composers to produce and digitally record, sweeten, mix, and edit much of their own music.

SCOR 523B.description: Advanced Screen Scoring Technology. Explores sophisticated principles and applications of technologies for screen scoring, including the use of synthesizers, samplers, and sequencers.

SCOR 590.description: Directed Research. Research leading to the Master's Degree. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

SCOR 790.description: Research. Research leading to the doctorate. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department.

SLL 199.description: Chess and Critical Thinking. Analysis of significant chess games, reflecting societal attitudes  towards science, competition, art, gender, psychology, politics,  and technology.  Graded CR/NC.

SLL 225.description: Intermediate Polish II. Intermediate level vocabulary and grammar related to topics such as bureaucracy, politics, law, ecology, culture and current affairs.

SLL 299.description: Chess - Advanced Thinking Techniques. Development of advanced understanding of the game of chess. Critical analysis of games and of the problem-solving techniques applicable in various game situations. Graded CR/NC.

SLL 344.description: Tolstoy: Writer and Moralist.  Tolstoy's major works in the context of his ethical views.Readings and lectures in English.

SLL 348.description: The Novels of Vladimir Nabokov. Survey of Vladimir Nabokov's novels written in Europe and Americafrom the 1920s - 1960s. Primary focus on the structure of thenovels and their themes of art and emigration. Readings inEnglish.

SLL 490.description: Directed Research.  Individual research and readings. Not available for graduate credit.

SLL 542.description: Symbolism.  Russian symbolist literature; cultural and philosophical background of this late 19th and early 20th century movement. Prerequisite: three years of college Russian.

SLL 545.description: 19th Century Russian Poetry. Analysis of major works of nineteenth century Russian poetry in the context of developing aesthetic principles and cultural history. Prereq: 501 or consent of instructor.

SOWK 200.description: Systemic Challenges and Social Change in the United States. Historical and philosophical foundations of social conditions in the United States and their implications for public policy.

SOWK 210.description: Global Well-being and Human Performance. Examines mindbody foundations of wellness and performance, analyzing motivation, stress, identity and social determinants to support equitable, culturally responsive approaches to thriving globally.

SOWK 300.description: Foundations of Social Work. Explore foundations of social work in this introductory course:    history, ethics, roles, communication, cultural competence,        advocacy and human rights.

SOWK 310.description: Technology for Global Good. In-class learning and asynchronous experiences to develop collaborative, sustainable and technology-based solutions to address global injustices.

SOWK 324.description: Juvenile Justice in America. The historical and current context of America's juvenile justice system and its influence on children, youth and families.

SOWK 336.description: Social Work Policy Advocacy for Social Change. Empower yourself for impactful change. Dive into policy advocacy as a social worker, exploring key concepts and strategies for social change.

SOWK 346.description: Evidence-Based Social Work Practice (EBSWP). Introduces undergraduates to evidence-based social work practice, including empirical research, AI/data tools and simulation modeling for data-driven interventions in social work settings.

SOWK 350.description: Adolescent Gang Intervention. The incidence of gangs (particularly in the Los Angeles area),  gang interventions, and policies developed to address the growing  gang situation.

SOWK 506.description: Human Behavior and the Social Environment. The person-in-environment, bio-psycho-social perspective is the lens through which theories of personality, family, group, organization, community, culture and their interactions are explored. (Duplicates credit in SOWK 503 and SOWK 505)

SOWK 510.description: Professional Self-Care in Integrative Social Work Practice. Focuses on the value, examination and integration of professional self-care, wellness and resilience strategies into ethical and professional integrative social work practice.

SOWK 511.description: Critical Decision Making in Integrative Social Work Practice. Focuses on the value and application of critical thinking and decision-making into ethical and professional integrative social work practice.

SOWK 525.description: Foundations of Integrative Social Work Practice II. Principles underlying social work practice with emphasis on intervention, termination and evaluation with individuals, families and groups though a social change framework.

SOWK 536.description: Policy and Advocacy in Professional Social Work. A study of the complex and interconnecting systems of policy, programs and communities that directly and indirectly impact Social Workers' clients lives. (Duplicates credit in SOWK 534)

SOWK 546.description: Science of Social Work. Introduction to the role of scientific inquiry in advancing social work goals. Inspires students to include science in their social work identity and professional decision-making. (Duplicates credit in SOWK 562)

SOWK 593.description: Applied Learning in Practicum Education II. Practicum seminar and placement for developing foundational skills in integrative social work practice with individuals, families, groups, communities and/or organizations.

SOWK 603.description: The Transforming Power of Social Work and Sports. The power of social work and sports to promote well-being, inclusivity and personal growth. This dynamic partnership fosters positive change within individuals, communities and society.

SOWK 609.description: Advanced ISW Practice II: Schools and Educational Settings. Critical application of theory, evidence and professional standards for integrative and culturally responsive assessment and intervention, highlighting practice contexts involving schools and educational settings

SOWK 612.description: Assessment and Diagnosis of Mental Disorders. Assessment of mental disorders, and the rationale and organization of the system for diagnosis. Emphasis is on developing differential diagnostic skills.

SOWK 615.description: Brief Therapy and Crisis Intervention. Theory and multimodal approaches for brief therapy and crisis intervention with a broad spectrum of clients in a range of mental health and health settings.

SOWK 617.description: Substance Related and Behavioral Addictive Disorders and Rec. Causal exploration of substance related and behavioral addictive disorders. Evidence-based and practice informed treatment models for vulnerable individuals, groups and families.

SOWK 630.description: Self-Awareness and Intercultural Humility in  Social Work. Critical exploration of sociocultural context and one's own  values/assumptions/biases to enhance intercultural humility in  social work.

SOWK 642.description: Advanced ISW Practice II: Children, Youth and Families. Critical application of theory, evidence and professional standards for integrative and culturally responsive assessment and intervention, highlighting practice contexts involving children, youth and families.

SOWK 647.description: Advanced ISW Practice II: Adult Mental Health and Wellness. Critical application of theory, evidence and professional standards for integrative and culturally responsive assessment and intervention, highlighting practice contexts involving adult mental health and wellness.

SOWK 651.description: Clinical Psychopharmacology for Social Workers. Understanding major psychoactive drugs used in treatment of psychological and behavioral disorders in behavioral and primary care medical settings. Theoretical/practical approaches to treatment are examined.

SOWK 656.description: National Military Immersion in Washington, DC: Military and . A short study at the campus, online, and in Washington, DC addressing policies and programs for military members, veterans, and their families.

SOWK 677.description: Mental Health Assessment and Diagnosis of Children and Adole. Mental health assessment and diagnosis of children and adolescents. Course includes relevant diagnoses and the systematic or societal challenges that impact mental health of youth.

SOWK 693.description: Applied Learning in Practicum Education IV. Practicum seminar and placement for developing advanced skills in integrative social work practice with individuals, families, groups, communities and/or organizations.

SOWK 697.description: Advanced Clinical Social Work Practice Certificate Lab. Clinical practice lab designed to strengthen clinical social work practice skills grounded in professional values and ethics.

SOWK 704.description: Complex Social Problems. Emphasizes leadership in addressing systemic social challenges.

SOWK 705.description: Leadership and Strategic Communication for Stakeholder Engag. Leading public discourse for the purposes of increasing civic engagement and public participation, building broad based public support and enabling competencies.

SOWK 706.description: Leadership for Intervention Implementation in Complex System. Examining large scale national, state and local intervention programs as well as modeling potential organizational redesign to improve service delivery strategies.

SOWK 707.description: Financial Management for Social Change. Senior financial management and planning in human service organizations, emphasizing fiscal approaches that focus on strategy, including how to maximize revenue, control costs, allocate resources, improve decision-making and support successful social programs and disruptive social change.

SOWK 711.description: Design Laboratory for Social Innovation I. Incorporates leadership in intervention design, stakeholder engagement, and evidence-based practices.

SOWK 713.description: Research Methods for Intervention Design and Evaluation. Introduction to doctoral-level applied research and evaluation methods, emphasizing the selection, design and application of methods for intervention design and evaluation in complex social contexts.

SOWK 714.description: Executive Leadership: Leaders as Maestros. The Leader/Maestro Concept enlarges the student from a virtuoso perspective - individual performance - to include an organizational performance in leading, creating and measuring change.

SOWK 716.description: Leadership in Complex Social Problem Identification. Develops advanced skills to define complex social problems through interdisciplinary, systems, and evidence-based analysis, identifying root causes, gaps, and implications that guide capstone solution design.

SOWK 717.description: Stakeholder Engagement and Solutions. Prepares students to lead stakeholder-informed inquiry and identify feasible, values-aligned solutions to complex social problems by deepening understanding of problem and solution landscapes.

SOWK 720.description: Leadership Communication for Social Impact. Mastering communication for social impact. Students will learn the power of listening, consensus-based facilitation, storytelling for social change and communicating with brevity.

SOWK 721.description: Data Driven Decision Making in Social Services. Practical introduction to using quantitative administrative data to identify trends, track performance, evaluate programs and drive decision making.

SOWK 723.description: Design Laboratory for Social Innovation II. Emphasizes leadership in developing responsive interventions to address complex social problems.

SOWK 725A.description: Preparatory Scholarship for Capstone. Design and develop an innovative, feasible, and defensible Capstone Project focusing on a selected Grand Challenge for Social Work.

SOWK 725B.description: Preparatory Scholarship for Capstone. Refine a fully implementable, innovatively designed Grand Challenge Capstone Project. Future-focused on garnering support, piloting and launching students' capstone prototype.

SOWK 725C.description: Preparatory Scholarship for Capstone. Complete a fully implementable, innovatively designed Grand Challenge Capstone Project. Future-focused on garnering support, piloting and launching students' capstone project.

SOWK 733.description: Policy Analysis and Advocacy in a Comparative Social Policy Context. Examination of the evolution of American and other welfare states  in selected nations.  Analysis of global welfare institutions.   Engaging in policy analysis in a comparative context.

SOWK 743.description: Applying Theory in Intervention Research. Doctoral seminar on applying behavioral theory across research     stages, from conceptualization to implementation, with focus on    intervention design, and real-world application in social work.

SOWK 763.description: Social Work Research Methods II: Issues in Research for Soci. Building on SOWK 762, deepens students' knowledge of social work research methods and strengthens their ability to develop original and rigorous research proposals.

SOWK 764.description: Statistics in Social Work II: Categorical Data Analysis. Introduction to single equation statistical modeling using limited dependent variables, including dichotomous, ordered categorical and other outcome forms. Methods are drawn from statistics and econometrics.

SOWK 765.description: Writing Successful Dissertation Research Grants. Prepares doctoral students to write and submit applications to obtain extramural funding to support their dissertation research. Students will learn about opportunities and eligibility requirements for federal and foundation supported dissertation research grants, how grants are reviewed and scored once submitted, and how to write successful proposals. Recommended preparation: Completion of a qualitative or mixed methods course is preferred.

SOWK 783.description: Doctoral Seminar II: Independent Scholarly Trajectories. Enhance students scholarly skills that are critical for becoming an independent scholar. Prepare students for their qualifying exam.

SOWK 784.description: Teaching Foundations in Social Work: Pedagogy  and Reflection. Teaching practices for future Social Work educators. Topics include teaching philosophy, lesson planning, and addressing common classroom challenges.

SOWK 794A.description: Doctoral Dissertation.  Credit on acceptance of dissertation.

SOWK 794B.description: Doctoral Dissertation.  Credit on acceptance of dissertation.

SOWK 794C.description: Doctoral Dissertation.  Credit on acceptance of dissertation.

SOWK 794D.description: Doctoral Dissertation.  Credit on acceptance of dissertation.

SOCI 150.description: Social Problems. Identifying and analyzing contemporary American social problems, their causes and potential solutions; examines poverty, crime, inequality, education, social isolation and civic decline.

SOCI 169.description: Changing Family Forms. The peculiarity of the "modern" Western family system in historical and cross-cultural perspective; focus on the "postmodern" family crisis in the United States.

SOCI 200.description: Introduction to Sociology.  Basic concepts of sociology with special reference to group life,social institutions, and social processes.

SOCI 210.description: Science, Technology, and Social Conflict. Science and technology change society and how we understand ourselves. In turn, social struggles influence science. We will explore the interplay between these forces.

SOCI 235.description: Migration, Law and Society. Migration policies worldwide are negotiated by different stakeholders and create different contexts of reception that differently impact the everyday lives and livelihoods of migrants.

SOCI 242.description: Sociology, Demography and Health. Sociological and demographic concepts focusing on the causes of disease, health and wellness. Empirical analysis of population composition and its connection to health.

SOCI 250.description: Grassroots Participation in Global Perspective. Theory and history behind the ideal of "the local, grassroots volunteer": a direct link between theory and research using Los Angeles as a case study.

SOCI 270.description: Sociological Theory. Historical and contemporary approaches to sociological theory; analysis of conceptual frameworks applied to the study of society and social interaction.

SOCI 313.description: Sociological Research Methods. Logic of theory construction, research design, elementary data collection and analysis.

SOCI 314.description: Analyzing Social Statistics. Sociological measurement, univariate description, elementary correlation, introduction to statistical inference.

SOCI 325.description: Applied Social Research Methods. Use quantitative or qualitative analysis skills to study major social issues using large existing survey data sets or qualitative methods. Become conversant in describing data to a variety of audiences.

SOCI 340.description: Organizations: Bureaucracy and Alternatives to Bureaucracy. Importance of organizations in social life; applied analysis of everyday bureaucratic and nonbureaucratic organizational structures; techniques for using and changing organizations.

SOCI 350.description: Social Exclusion, Social Power and Deviance. Examines meanings of deviance and connection with status, power, and social control. Topics include homelessness, mental health, sexuality, the body, drugs, gambling and corporate crime.

SOCI 360.description: Social Inequality: Class, Status and Power. Inequalities in wealth, prestige and power in the United States; the American class structure and the extent of upward mobility in that structure.

SOCI 369.description: The Family in a Changing Society. Changing family patterns; personality development; family unity, predicting success in marriage; the family in transition; crises such as economic changes, death, divorce; family reorganization.

SOCI 425.description: Social Movements: Power, Resistance and Political Dynamics. When do groups mobilize to defend or resist power? Explores collective mobilization including student protest, minority rights and labor movements, the alt-right and revolutions.

SOCI 440.description: Environmental Sociology. Explores the causes and possible solutions to the environmental crisis, with emphasis on the politics of environmental knowledge and regulation.

SOCI 475.description: Medical Sociology.  Social and cultural factors in causation of disease, health care utilization and health care delivery.

SOCI 490.description: Directed Research.  Individual research and readings. Not available for graduate credit.

SOCI 511.description: Sociological Theory II. Developments in sociological theory from World War II to the present. Duplicates credit in former SOCI 610.

SOCI 520.description: Qualitative Research Methods. Seminar in epistemologies, ethics, and techniques of qualitative  research.  Critical reading and practice in social observation,  interviewing, fieldwork, and research design.  Preparation of IRB  proposal.

SOCI 590.description: Directed Research.  Research leading to the master's degree. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

SOCI 594A.description: Master's Thesis.  Credit on acceptance of thesis.

SOCI 594B.description: Master's Thesis.  Credit on acceptance of thesis.

SOCI 621.description: Quantitative Methods and Statistics II. Casual modeling and the inter-relationships among social phenomena: covers the basic elements of casual inference and generalizability, linear regressions analysis, and categorical data analysis.

SOCI 651.description: Seminar in Social Stratification. Critique of research literature and research methods in the area of social class and social stratification; major theories and theoretical implications of current research. Duplicates credit in former SOCI 551.

SOCI 657.description: Sociology of Culture. Cultural theories and forms of cultural analysis appropriate for sociological research; critical examination of theory and research on how culture relates to social structure, social inequality, politics, institutions, and everyday interaction. Recommended preparation: SOCI 510 or prior undergraduate or graduate coursework in social science or communication studies. Duplicates credit in former SOCI 535.

SOCI 675.description: Seminar in Immigration. Survey of key theoretical approaches and relevant issues in immigration studies. Themes include: transationalism, globalization, gendered migration, segmented assimilation, immigrant labor markets, social incorporation and citizenship. Open to Ph.D. in Sociology students only. Duplicates credit in former SOCI 575.

SOCI 680.description: Writing for Publication in Sociology. Prepares graduate students to publish in peer reviewed journals. Prerequisite: SOCI 620 or SOCI 622. Graded CR/NC.

SOCI 790.description: Research.  Research leading to the doctorate. Maximum units which may be     applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded   CR/NC.

SOCI 794B.description: Doctoral Dissertation.  Credit on acceptance of dissertation.

SPAN 120.description: Spanish I.  For students with limited proficiency in Spanish. Practice in     listening comprehension, oral communication, elementary reading    and writing.

SPAN 150.description: Spanish II. Continuation of Spanish 110 or 120; increased emphasis on listening comprehension, oral expression, reading and writing.

SPAN 220.description: Spanish III. Continuation of SPAN 150; intensive work in listening comprehension, oral communication, reading, and writing with emphasis on free expression; readings related to Hispanic culture and civilization. Prereq: SPAN 150 or equivalent.

SPAN 240.description: Spanish IV. Intensive review of Spanish grammar with emphasis on four skills. Audio-visual materials and readings related to Hispanic culture and civilization.

SPAN 260.description: Advanced Spanish: Arts and Sciences.  Development of students' oral and writing skills using literary and scientific materials; grammar review. Duplicates credit in the former SPAN 266.

SPAN 270.description: Spanish for Heritage Speakers. Culture-based course designed for Spanish speakers not formally trained in the language. Review language and grammar and hone presentational skills.

SPAN 280.description: Conversational Spanish. Discussions of short films, cultural and literary texts and other activities designed to improve conversational skills. Prerequisite: SPAN 220. Not for credit for Spanish majors.

SPAN 295.description: Gender and Sexuality in Latin American and Spanish Cinema. Examines the representation of gender and sexual discourses and  the intersection with wider social, political and theoretical  issues in Latin American and Spanish cinema. Taught in English.

SPAN 301.description: Introduction to Literature and Film. Introduction to critical reading and interpretation of poetry, narrative fiction, drama and film from Spain and Latin America.

SPAN 304.description: The Art of Fiction. A survey of Spanish and Latin American fiction from the Middle Ages to the present, acquainting students with various critical and theoretical approaches to narrative. Conducted in Spanish.

SPAN 315.description: Advanced Grammar and Translation. Contrastive study of Spanish and English structures designed to explore the similarities and differences between the two languages and to familiarize students with translation techniques. Emphasis on a variety of text types with the aim of increasing linguistic and cultural appreciation of the Spanish language.

SPAN 316.description: Spanish for the Professions. The language and culture of a particular area of study or profession, such as medicine and healthcare, political and social sciences, business and the law. Limited to 4 units for major or minor credit.

SPAN 380.description: Literature of Mexico. Principal writers and their works from Colonial times to the present. Non-majors may write assignments in English. Recommended preparation: advanced comprehension of oral and written Spanish.

SPAN 385.description: The Culture of Food in Hispanic Los Angeles. Experiential learning and project-based course designed to familiarize students with the food culture of Hispanic Los Angeles. Students create Spanish language blogs about their experiences.

SPAN 483.description: Gender and Sexuality. An examination of gender, sexuality, and power in Iberian and Latin American literatures and cultures.  Conducted in Spanish.

SPAN 490.description: Directed Research.  Individual research and readings. Not available for graduate credit.

SPAN 501.description: Cultural Narratives of Spain and Latin America. Theoretical and methodological approaches to cultural narratives in Spanish and Latin American literary and cultural studies.

SPAN 602.description: Seminar in Spanish and Latin American Critical Theory. Major developments in literary criticism in Spain and Latin America from the early modern period to the present.

SSCI 135.description: Maps in the Digital World. The role of formal reasoning, abstract representation and empirical analysis in building maps for sharing knowledge across the physical, life and social sciences and humanities.

SSCI 165.description: Sustainability Science in the City. The influence of sustainability science on public policy and vice versa in the context of social/ethical theories, analytical methods and solutions.

SSCI 201.description: Principles of Geodesign. Foundations of geodesign combining place-making, design, collective action, and the science of location-based information to improve human interaction with the functioning of the Earth.

SSCI 214.description: Human Populations and Natural Hazards. Introduction to the complex relationship between human development and natural hazards, which are increasingly causing damage and displacement to human populations throughout the world.

SSCI 265.description: The Water Planet. An exploration of earth's water, ranging from water properties, chemistry, and pollution, to groundwater dynamics, watershed processes, and oceanic-atmospheric circulation. Implications for past and future societies. Lecture and laboratory.

SSCI 301.description: Maps and Spatial Reasoning. Role of maps and spatial reasoning in the production and use of geographic information for representing and analyzing human and environmental activities and events.

SSCI 315.description: 3D GIS and Geodesign. Integrated 3D GIS, CAD, and BIM workflows for geodesign, spatial analytics, and digital twins to support data-driven urban and environmental decision-making.

SSCI 350.description: International Geodesign. Intensive living-learning research and field experience in Los Angeles and abroad; application of geodesign strategies to local societal challenges.

SSCI 382.description: Geographic Information Science: Spatial Analytics. The various ways in which geography can be used to acquire, represent, organize, analyze, model and visualize information. Laboratories are organized around ArcGIS software suite.

SSCI 383.description: Geographic Information Science: Geospatial Modeling and Cust. Fundamentals of spatial modeling and remote sensing and how to use GIS customization and programming to streamline complex spatial analysis and modeling workflows.

SSCI 397.description: Spatial Sciences Internship. Intensive experience in local public agency, private firm, or nonprofit agency engaged in applied geospatial analysis, modeling and mapping work.

SSCI 420.description: Human Security and Geospatial Intelligence Practicum. Create conceptual solutions for a real-world human security and geospatial intelligence issue by developing a problem set and recommended solution to the same.

SSCI 490.description: Directed Research.  Individual research and readings. Open only to juniors and seniors. Not available for graduate credit.

SSCI 575.description: Spatial Data Science. Introduce the spatial data scientific approach to issues and present a holistic generalizable analysis pipeline.

SSCI 579.description: Geospatial Intelligence Tradecraft. Typical geospatial intelligence tasks and their use in military operations, national and homeland security, international relief work and disaster management. Recommended preparation: SSCI-581.

SSCI 581.description: Concepts for Spatial Thinking. The unique characteristics and importance of spatial information as they relate to the evolving science, technology, and applications of Geographic Information Systems.

SSCI 582.description: Spatial Databases. Design, implementation, and interrogation of relational, object-oriented and other types of geospatial databases. Recommended preparation: SSCI 581.

SSCI 583.description: Spatial Analysis and Modeling. Provides the knowledge and skills necessary to investigate the spatial patterns which result from social and physical processes operating at or near the Earth's surface.

SSCI 585.description: Geospatial Technology Project Management. Concepts, principles, and use of project management tools and the people issues encountered running GIS projects. Recommended preparation: SSCI 581.

SSCI 586.description: GIS Programming and Customization. Design, coding, and implementation of GIS-based software and models using the Python programming language. Recommended preparation: SSCI 582. Duplicates credit in former GEOG 586.

SSCI 587.description: Spatial Data Acquisition. Role of global positioning systems, maps, geocoding, and other kinds of sensors as geospatial data sources. Includes field data acquisition excursion on Catalina Island. Recommended preparation: SSCI-581. Duplicates credit in former GEOG 587.

SSCI 589.description: Cartography and Visualization. Principles of visual perception, spatial cognition and cartographic design and their contributions to the maps, animations, virtual reality and multimedia displays produced with modern GIS. Recommended preparation: SSCI 581.

SSCI 590.description: Directed Research.  Research leading to the master's degree in cognate fields. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

SSCI 594A.description: Master's Thesis. Credit on acceptance of thesis. Graded CR/NC.

SSCI 594B.description: Master's Thesis. Credit on acceptance of thesis. Graded CR/NC.

SSCI 594Z.description: Master's Thesis. Credit on acceptance of thesis. Graded CR/NC.

SSCI 595.description: Applied Geospatial Intelligence Problem Solving. Provides hands-on problem solving opportunity that requires knowledge and GEOINT skills to provide an informed recommendation involving a variety of human security settings.

SSCI 596.description: Internship in Spatial Sciences. Part-time or full-time practical work experience in the student's field of study at an off-campus facility under faculty direction.

SSCI 680.description: Advanced Spatial Computing. The role of spatial computing in understanding the world, in knowing and communicating our relationships to specific places, and for navigating through those places.

SSCI 683.description: Principles of Spatial Data Analysis. The theoretical foundations and techniques of spatial analysis and the ways in which they have been used to identify spatial processes and patterns. Recommended preparation: Enrollment in a USC PhD Program.

SSCI 684.description: Spatial Modeling with GIS. An introduction to spatial models identifying the key issues influencing the success of these models in simulating key social and environmental processes and health exposures.

SSCI 790.description: Research. Research leading to the doctoral degree. Maximum units which may  be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Open  only to doctoral students.

SSCI 794A.description: Doctoral Dissertation. Credit on acceptance of Dissertation. Open only to doctoral students in Population, Health, and Place major. Graded: IP/CR/NC.

SSCI 794B.description: Doctoral Dissertation. Credit on acceptance of Dissertation. Open only to doctoral students in Population, Health, and Place major. Graded: IP/CR/NC.

SSCI 794C.description: Doctoral Dissertation. Credit on acceptance of Dissertation. Open only to doctoral students in Population, Health, and Place major. Graded: IP/CR/NC.

SSCI 794D.description: Doctoral Dissertation. Credit on acceptance of Dissertation. Open only to doctoral students in Population, Health, and Place major. Graded: IP/CR/NC.

SSCI 794Z.description: Doctoral Dissertation. Credit on acceptance of Dissertation. Open only to doctoral students in Population, Health, and Place major. Graded: IP/CR/NC.

SCRM 388.description: Gene Editing and Gene Therapy. Overview of gene editing technologies and their applications in vitro and in vivo to advancements in disease modeling and clinical therapies for patients.

SCRM 490.description: Directed Research. Individual research and readings under the guidance of a faculty member.

SCRM 510.description: Current Topics in Regenerative Medicine. Selected topics on sub-fields within developmental and stem cell biology including review of contemporary literature and research.

SCRM 515.description: Bringing Stem Cells to the Clinic. Lectures addressing the business, legal, ethical, manufacturing and regulatory aspects involved in moving stem cells or related product into clinical practice.

SCRM 517.description: Historical and Contemporary Stem Cell Research. Historical and contemporary stem cell research using hematopoietic stem cells as a model system.

SCRM 519.description: Historical and Contemporary Research: Neural Stem Cells. Focuses on historic achievements in stem cell research and how contemporarily, research and its related technological advances have fostered breakthroughs the understanding of NSCs.

SCRM 521.description: Historical and Contemporary Research: Tissue Development Eng. Focuses on the components of cell, molecular biology, and basic tissue development to comprehend its uses within the realm of synthetic biology and cellular/tissue engineering.

SCRM 524.description: Culture and Differentiation of Pluripotent Stem Cells. Classroom and laboratory experience in the techniques for deriving, culturing and differentiating pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) and related cell types.

SCRM 526.description: Data Analysis in Stem Cell Biology. Training in the analytical tools needed to assess data-sets typically acquired during stem cell biology research.

SCRM 580.description: SCRM External Speaker Seminar Series. Reading and discussion of recent papers by the SCRM speaker of the week, and attendance at the speaker's seminar. Open only to Stem Cell Biology and Regenerative Medicine majors.

SCRM 590.description: Independent Research. Independent research conducted under the guidance of faculty in the Department of Stem Cell Biology and Regenerative Medicine.

SCRM 594A.description: Master's Thesis. Credit on acceptance of Thesis. Graded IP/CR/NC.

SCRM 594B.description: Master's Thesis. Credit on acceptance of Thesis. Graded IP/CR/NC.

SCRM 594Z.description: Master's Thesis. Credit on acceptance of Thesis. Graded IP/CR/NC.

SMGT 500.description: Introduction to Sustainability. History and evolution of sustainability, including definitions, models and policies relevant to current global sustainability and advocacy.

SMGT 505.description: Sustainability Fundamentals. Evolution of business sustainability; environmental, social and governance (ESG) performance; and the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

SMGT 510.description: Business Strategy for a Sustainable World. Business strategies, practices, and performance metrics that champion sustainability as part of organizational purpose.

SMGT 515.description: Leading Organizational Transformation for Sustainability. Organizational transformation through integration of sustainability into values, culture, leadership, talent, workflow and strategy.

SMGT 520.description: Sustainable Supply and Global Value Chains. Sustainable management of supply chains and global value chains to increase benefits to business, the environment and society.

SMGT 525.description: The Circular Economy and Sustainable Design. Interrelationship of circular economy and sustainable design strategies to reduce waste and negative social and environmental impacts.

SMGT 530.description: Sustainable Finance and Capital Markets. Sustainable investment and finance strategies for both investors and companies.

SMGT 535.description: Business Strategies for Addressing Climate Change. Principles of climate science and the role of business in mitigating the effects of a changing climate.

SMGT 550.description: Sustainability Metrics and Reporting. Strategies for organizations to identify, measure and report on prioritized sustainability issues.

SMGT 555.description: Sustainability Management Strategy Capstone. Knowledge and skills gained throughout the Sustainability Management program are synthesized in a culminating capstone project.

SAE 541.description: Systems Engineering Theory and Practice. Integration of engineering problem solving methodologies based on systems concepts. Application to complex, large scale technical systems and problems faced by engineering managers. Case studies.

SAE 542.description: Advanced Topics in Systems Engineering. Probability theory  in systems engineering: test design and performance, reliability and maintainability, quantitative decision models. Constraint theory to manage and de-conflict complex requirements. Complexity theory.

SAE 547.description: Model-Based Systems Architecting and Engineering. Approaches for modeling systems using software such as SySML; modeling system, requirements, structure, behavior, and parametrics; mapping to hardware description language and behavioral code generation. Recommended preparation: Modeling and simulation courses.

SAE 548.description: Systems/System-of-Systems Integration and Communication. Essentials of systems and system-of-systems integration from the perspectives of business, programs, and technology. Process, Legacy, and Systems-of-Systems Integration. Verification and Validation methods. Case studies. Recommended preparation: Bachelor's degree in engineering or physical sciences.

SAE 550.description: Systems Architecting and the Political Process                                                   . Analysis of risks inherent in managing high-tech/high-cost  government-funded engineering programs; tools and techniques for  coping with the impacts of politically-driven budgets on the      engineering design process.  Recommended preparation: 2 years of  work experience.

SAE 560.description: Economic Considerations for Systems Engineering. Impact of economic factors for systems architects and engineers,  tools for understanding these factors, fundamental quantitative  analysis of cash flow, life-cost estimating for systems and  software engineering.

SAE 580.description: Artificial Intelligence for Systems Engineers. Linear modeling, knowledge representation, supervised and unsupervised learning, optimization and evolutionary algorithms; augmented intelligence for decision-making, intelligent monitoring and control; real-world applications.

SAE 590.description: Directed Research. Research leading to the master's degree.  Maximum units which may  be applied to the degree to be determined by the department.   Graded CR/NC.
