TAC 100.description: Enhanced Productivity with AI. Enhance  how you think, work, and create by mastering AI tools that amplify focus, creativity, and personal productivity.

TAC 101.description: Business Tools and Digital Fluency. An introduction to the software and technologies used in modern business environments and practices required to effectively function in online environments.

TAC 104.description: Web Development. Core HTML and CSS for building functional, custom websites. Includes responsive design, modern frameworks and AI-assisted tools.

TAC 115.description: Programming in Python. Introduction to Python; intended for students without prior programming experience.

TAC 116.description: Accelerated Programming in Python. Accelerated introduction to Python; intended for students with prior programming experience.

TAC 125.description: Hackers to CEOs: Intro to Cyber Security in the AI Era. Cyber security, threats, intrusions, controls and countermeasures. Hacking computers and humans. Cyber and AI risk. Phishing, social engineering and other human hacking techniques.

TAC 165.description: Introduction to C++ Programming. Introduction to programming using C++, including variables, operators, conditionals, loops, arrays, vectors, strings, functions, files, structs, pointers, dynamic allocation and an introduction to classes.

TAC 168.description: Introduction to MATLAB. Fundamentals of MATLAB: a high-performance numeric computation and visualization environment. Overview of linear algebra and matrix manipulation; using 2-D and 3-D plotting routines; programming in MATLAB; basic numerical analysis.

TAC 181.description: Video Game QA Management. Survey of game software development through quality assurance and in-depth analysis of the development cycle with a focus on bug testing systems, methodologies and QA Management.

TAC 190.description: Digital Graphics and UI Design Tools. Learn tools for digital graphics and visual communication using Photoshop, with fundamentals supporting social media, print, presentations and UI design.

TAC 215.description: Introduction to 3D Modeling, Animation and Visual Effects. An applied introduction to the techniques used for modeling, animating, texturing, lighting, rendering, and creating 3D content for games, cinematics, visual effects, animation and visualizations.

TAC 216.description: Applied Python. Development of practical Python programming skills through project-based applications; "Pythonic" ways of solving problems in modern computational domains.

TAC 249.description: Introduction to Data Analytics. Introduction to data analytics. Basics of databases, applied statistics, data visualization. Leverage data to make critical business decisions.

TAC 259.description: Basics of Artificial Intelligence. Concepts and techniques in artificial intelligence; approaches in artificial narrow intelligence; applications of AI that are already changing society; ethical and social questions in AI.

TAC 265.description: Software Design with Object-Oriented Programming. Learn to design and build software systems using object-oriented programming, with a focus on modular thinking, problem solving and real-world applications across disciplines.

TAC 298.description: Special Topics. Selected topics in Technology and Applied Computing.

TAC 301.description: Front-End Web Development. Covers programming fundamentals, client-side programming, dynamic UI manipulation, modern frameworks and libraries and the use of AI-assisted tools in front-end development.

TAC 303.description: Full-Stack Web Development. Modern web development techniques for building web applications from the ground up. Front-end and back-end development, including databases, JavaScript libraries and web application frameworks.

TAC 325.description: Ethical Hacking. Ethical hacking; penetration testing; vulnerability assessment; red teams; hacker environments, infrastructure and frameworks; lateral movement and data exfiltration techniques; evasion and anti-forensics.

TAC 348.description: Making Smart Devices: Introduction to Electronics/Wearables. Design of electronic devices that interact with the physical world; electronic interfaces; development of software algorithms; micro-controller implementation.

TAC 357.description: Enterprise Networks: Design and Architecture. Network technologies. Routers and managed switches. Integrated operating systems (IOS). Strategies for endpoint management. Subnets and securing subnetworks. Reliability with networks and network infrastructure.

TAC 359.description: Applied Neural Networks. Design, build, and train applied neural networks to solve real-world problems; implement neural networks for machine vision, image recognition and object detection and tracking.

TAC 361.description: Character Rigging for Games. Fundamentals of character rigging for video game production and development; optimization of character design, skeleton and mass properties for effective rigging; virtual rigs.

TAC 370.description: Cybersecurity Management and Operations. Cybersecurity project design. Incident response. Teambuilding, management and communications for cybersecurity. Scalable approaches for implementation of Information Security Management Systems.

TAC 375.description: Digital Forensics and Cybersecurity Investigations. Forensic science techniques. Digital evidence preservation. Processes and methodologies for digital examinations. Cyber crime investigations. Windows file system analysis. Real case scenario analysis and reporting

TAC 376.description: Engineering AI Products. Full-stack engineering of Al-native products from system architecture to deployment and employing the modern technical stack to transform concepts into market-ready software.

TAC 388.description: Developing Smart Devices. From prototype to PCB to funding pitch: building internet-connected smart devices. Design, fabricate, assemble and test a smart device of your own conceptualization.

TAC 393.description: Video Game Project Management. Production and project management of video games from concept to release and beyond.

TAC 443.description: Malware Analysis and Reverse Engineering. Reverse engineering concepts for malware analysis; debuggers and decompilers; static and dynamic analysis of malicious scripts and binaries; focused on Windows and Windows APls.

TAC 447.description: Mobile Device Forensics and Security. Digital forensics, evidence extraction and analysis of mobile devices (Android, iOS and Blackberry), Cellular networks, IoT devices and legacy mobile and hand-held devices.

TAC 459.description: Applied Natural Language Processing and Generative AI. Generative AI and NLP fundamentals through hands-on work with GPT/BERT, covering prompt engineering, RAG, fine-tuning, retrieval, sentiment analysis, QA and machine translation for product building.

TAC 466.description: Building the High Tech Startup. Startup creation: idea and team development, market strategy, business models, financial planning, go-to-market approaches, product development, agile methods and core organizational building skills.

TAC 470.description: Technology and Applied Computing Practicum. Independent technology project related to specific topics under    the direction of a faculty member.

TAC 479.description: Cyber Law and Privacy. Cyber legal issues, search and seizure, 4th amendment and digital evidence, warrants, private searches, wiretaps, tracking devices, workplace privacy.

TAC 480.description: Technology and Applied Computing Internship. Practical experience in applying information technology skills in  real-world settings. Supervised internship at companies and        start-ups. Balancing academic rigor with corporate challenges and  deadlines.

GRSC 800A.description: Studies for the Qualifying Examination. Studies for the Qualifying Examination. Students may enroll in GRSC 800, once they have completed all other degree requirements, to prepare for their Qualifying Examination.

GRSC 800B.description: Studies for the Qualifying Examination. Studies for the Qualifying Examination. Students may enroll in GRSC 800, once they have completed all other degree requirements, to prepare for their Qualifying Examination.

GRSC 803.description: Enrollment for PhD Students on an Approved Health Leave                      . This course is administratively created to ensure continuing PhD  students have access to health insurance and other support while  on an approved health leave.

GRSC 804.description: Enrollment for PhD students on an Approved       Parental Leave                                  . This course is administratively created to ensure continuing PhD  students have access to health insurance and other support while  on an approved parental leave.

GRSC 810.description: Studies for Master's Examination. Completion of all course work for the master's degree and  permission of the Graduate School.  Graded CR/NC.

CORE 101.description: Symbols and Conceptual Systems: Thematic Option Honors Progr. Study of the structures through which we shape our experience in religion, philosophy, literature, music, and the visual arts, and of competing theories of interpretation. Students may not take this course on a P/NP basis.

CORE 103.description: The Process of Change in Science: Thematic Option Honors Pro. Critical problems in the development of scientific thought, studied as vehicles for understanding the content and structure of the sciences. Specific subject matter in selected scientific disciplines will be presented. Students may not take this course on a P/NP basis.

CORE 104.description: Change and the Future: Thematic Option Honors Program. Analysis of historical change; social and political theory and revolutionary thought; introduction to competing images of future states of affairs; the continuing process of change. Students may not take this course on a P/NP basis.

CORE 112.description: Writing Seminar II: Thematic Option Honors Program. Instruction on analytic writing that integrates methods of research, identifying and addressing specific audiences and  presenting ideas publicly. Readings examine  modernity and postmodernity.

CORE 200.description: Liberal Arts Reading Salon. Critical readings of a series of texts in the liberal arts  designed to promote discussion of important themes, theoretical  approaches, research directions, and interdisciplinary  connections.  Graded CR/NC.

CORE 499.description: Special Topics.  Intensive interdisciplinary exploration of a selected theme, problem, process, or period.

CORE 601.description: Teaching Analytical Writing through Readings in the Humanities. Theories and practices in university-level teaching of  close-reading and analytical writing, using texts central to  Western tradition.  Graduate student professionalization throught  topical workshops and discussions.  Open to assistant lecturers  and teaching assistants only.  Graded CR/NC.

TRGN 515.description: Advanced Human Genomic Analysis Methods. Molecular biotechnology, genomics, next-generation sequencing,  epigenomics, drug discovery, biomarkers, microarrays, analytical  validation, pipelines, molecular analysis.

TRGN 520.description: Translational Biomedical Informatics Capstone Portfolio. Portfolio, translational biomedical informatics, bioinformatics, genomics, application development, web-based application.

TRGN 527.description: Applied Data Science and Bioinformatics. Data science and bioinformatics tools in the study of human health and disease using R and Bioconductor for students from non-quantitative backgrounds.

TRGN 537.description: Pathway and Target Discovery. Exploration of the process of discovering and developing novel therapeutic treatments.

TRGN 538.description: Seminar in Translational Biotechnology. Series of seminars that provide updated views on various sub-specialties in biotechnology.

TRGN 539.description: Translational Biotechnology Practicum. Experiential training based on a project in a biomedical, biotechnology or pharmaceutical setting.

TRGN 540.description: Translational Biotechnology Capstone Preparation. Preparation for capstone defense course.

TRGN 541.description: Translational Biotechnology Capstone Defense. Finalization and defense of capstone project.

TRGN 544.description: Biotechnology Entrepreneurship and Commercialization II. Advanced discussion: global biotechnology industry, idea generation, business plan formulation, intellectual property protection, funding, personnel management including board composition, regulatory body interaction, company exits.

TRGN 546.description: Biotechnology Law: Intellectual Property, Regulatory, Corpor. Core concepts in intellectual property law, regulatory law, healthcare law, corporate law and M&A law to the biopharmaceutical and diagnostic device sectors. Open to students who are pursuing or have already attained graduate degrees (MS, PhD or PharmD) in the bioscience disciplines, or students from professional schools who have college-level bioscience background.

TRGN 551.description: Communicating Science: Speaking. Verbal communication modalities for accurate and effective transmission of scientific information to a wide audience in biomedical, healthcare, and related industries.

TRGN 590.description: Directed Research. Research leading to the master's degree. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department.

USC 500O.description: Off Campus Studies            . Off campus coursework; course serves as a block enrollment until  transcript from host institution is provided and can be  articulated into an MOI that results in individual courses on the  USC transcript with section titles that reflect the title of the  course at the host institution.

PLUS 653.description: Leading Change and Innovation in Urban Communities. In-depth study of the role of public, private, and non-profit leaders in effecting change in public policy and planning practice, with special attention to the goals and processes of social innovation in urban communities.

PLUS 694A.description: Planning, Design and Development Professional Dissertation . Credit on acceptance of Planning, Design and Development Professional Dissertation. Graded IP/CR/NC.

VISS 599.description: Special Topics. Special Topics in Visual Studies.

CTWR 206B.description: Writing the Screenplay. Writing a feature-length screenplay based on treatment developed in CTWR 206a. Includes a first draft and a polish.

CTWR 211.description: The Television Writer: An Agent of Change. The television writer as an agent of change across current social issues including, but not limited to: race, gender, and class.

CTWR 250.description: Breaking the Story . Examination of the fundamental elements of a good story, and how to use those elements to develop new screenplay ideas. Recommended preparation: CTWR 106b.

CTWR 321.description: Breaking the Hour-Long Television Series. Introduction to hour-long television staff writing. Breaking of a complete season and writing episodes. Special attention to season construction, pitching, character and story engine.

CTWR 324.description: Breaking the Half-Hour Television Series. The fundamentals of writing for half-hour television. Writing an episode of an existing half-hour television series, with emphasis on conception, pitching, characterization and structure.

CTWR 400.description: Is This A Joke: Mechanics of Comedy Writing. Intensive fundamental writing class for all forms of comedy writing including joke construction, late night, sketches, scene work, and stand-up.

CTWR 403.description: Writing the Narrative Podcast Series. Development of an original narrative podcast. Emphasis on dramatic elements of auditory storytelling and character development.

CTWR 406.description: Why The Long Face: Writing Comedy & the Human Experience. Lectures in Comedy Writing through an interdisciplinary exploration of human experience and expression in the genre.

CTWR 409.description: Fundamentals of Screenwriting: Character, Conflict and Story. Introduction to writing compelling scenes, creating authentic characters, three-act structure and feature film outlining.

CTWR 411.description: Television Script Analysis . In-depth analysis of the craft of writing prime-time episodic television. Examination of situation comedies and dramas through weekly screenings and lectures.

CTWR 413.description: Writing the Short Script I. Preparation of scripts for short films: form, structure, planning. Open only to Cinematic Arts Film and Television Production majors.

CTWR 414.description: The Screenplay. Students study story structure and develop several story outlines, write a short script for possible production, a feature film outline and first act. Recommended preparation: CTWR-416. Open only to Cinematic Arts Film and Television Production majors.

CTWR 417.description: Script Coverage and Story Analysis. Evaluation of completed scripts prior to their production.  Coverage and analysis of scripts as potential properties from the  perspective of a production company.

CTWR 418B.description: Senior Thesis. b: Completion and revision of Senior Thesis project and  introduction to motion picture industry procedures and practices through interaction with industry representatives.  Open to B.F.A. Writing for Screen and Television students only.

CTWR 419B.description: Senior Thesis in Dramatic Television . Revision of original pilot script, writing of mid-season episode, and completion of bible for original dramatic series developed in first semester.

CTWR 422.description: Creating the Dramatic Television Series . Examination and creation of the world, characters, and concept for an original hour-long dramatic series. Writing an outline for an original dramatic pilot.

CTWR 423.description: Writing the Screenplay. Introduction to formal elements of the screenplay through lectures and the workshopping of a complete first draft of a feature-length script.

CTWR 430.description: Comedy Writers and Their Work. Detailed investigation of specific comedy writers, comedy genres, and the works they've influenced. Lectures include screenings and visiting screenwriters.

CTWR 431.description: Screenwriters and Their Work. Detailed investigation of a specific screenwriter's style and the works they've influenced. Lectures include screenings and visiting screenwriters.

CTWR 432.description: Television Writers and Their Work. Detailed investigation of various television writers' styles, the worlds they have created, and the works they've influenced. Lectures include screenings and visiting television writers.

CTWR 437.description: Writing the Original Situation Comedy Pilot. Advanced workshop for writing an original half-hour comedy series, including a pilot script, summary of characters and story lines for first season.

CTWR 439.description: Writing the Original Dramatic Series Pilot. Advanced workshop in creation of an original dramatic series, including a first draft of the pilot and a summary of characters and storylines.

CTWR 446.description: Narrative Design of the Contained Story. Analysis and practice of storytelling techniques when faced with imposed story limitations.  Weekly screenings and lectures of classic and contemporary works.

CTWR 449.description: Rewriting the Original Dramatic Series Pilot. An advanced workshop in which an original hour-long television pilot will be rewritten with emphasis on character, world creation and future story lines. Prerequisite(s): CTWR 439. Recommended preparation: CTWR 411.

CTWR 453.description: Advanced Feature Rewriting. An advanced workshop in which a feature length screenplay will be rewritten using a specific methodology that focuses on a macro to micro approach to revision.

CTWR 457.description: Writing the Comedy Screenplay. Writing a comedy feature length screenplay. Special attention to creating comedic characters and premise. Outline and first draft.

CTWR 459A.description: Entertainment Industry Seminar. Examination and analysis of various topics, issues, and resources  pertaining to creative, legal, and business perspectives for  writers in the entertainment industry.

CTWR 505.description: Creating the Short Film. Strengthening and deepening the ability to conceive and develop  ideas that will lead to compelling, authentic, and personally  meaningful films.  Duplicates credit in CTWR 528.

CTWR 510.description: Fundamentals of Storytelling for Animation. Introduction to the fundamentals of storytelling with techniques and practices that work best for animated stories.

CTWR 514B.description: Basic Dramatic Screenwriting. Dramaturgy for the fiction and nonfiction work. Techniques for creating the original or adapted theatrical script. Open to graduate screenwriting majors (CTWR) and dramatic writing (Theatre) majors only. Development of an outline and feature-length original script.

CTWR 515B.description: Practicum in Screenwriting. Comprehensive re-writing of second and third drafts of a feature screenplay leading to a polished and professional piece.

CTWR 516.description: Advanced Motion Picture Script Analysis. Critical analysis of the structure of films from the classics to  current award winners.  Students will learn how to identify key  story concepts and break down three act structure in finished  films and scripts.

CTWR 517B.description: Thesis in Half-Hour Television Comedy. The re-write, casting, and performance stages of television comedy development. The completion of a final draft of the pilot script and series bible. Open only to Writing for Screen and Television master students.

CTWR 519B.description: Thesis in Television Drama. Part B -- writing the series bible and mid-season episode -- is  part two of the television thesis course.  Students develop their  original series further by writing the bible for the series and  the mid-season episode which is reflective of storylines,  characters and settings developed in part A of the course.  Open  to M.F.A. Writing for Screen and Television students only.

CTWR 520.description: Advanced Scene Writing Workshop. Intensive workshop oriented specifically to writing and rewriting the most effective and telling dramatic scenes to heighten audience participation and greater story impact.

CTWR 523.description: Introduction to the Screenplay. Introduction to formal elements of the screenplay through lectures and the workshopping of a complete first draft of a feature-length script. Prerequisite: CTAN 536 or CTWR 505 or CTWR 518. Recommended preparation: CTWR 516.

CTWR 529.description: Intermediate Screenwriting. Emphasizes structural elements crucial to the feature film. Techniques for creating an original or adapted theatrical-length script.

CTWR 533.description: Rewriting the Feature Screenplay. Rewriting the feature-length screenplay.  Focus on macro to micro approach to revision.

CTWR 537.description: Advanced Half-Hour Comedy Series Pilot. Development of an original half-hour comedy series; writing of the pilot episode and series bible.

CTWR 539.description: Advanced Hour-Long Drama Series Pilot. Development of an original one hour drama series; writing of the pilot episode and series bible.

CTWR 541.description: Dreams, the Brain, and Storytelling. Examination of the links between the brain, creativity, neuroscience and storytelling. Through lectures, screenings, and readings, students will log dreams for use in creative exercises.

CTWR 555.description: Pitching for Film and Television. Development and pitching of ideas for motion pictures, episodic, and television pilots. Reducing ideas to basic components enhancing verbal presentation skills.

CTWR 585.description: Advanced Genre Writing. Development and execution of writing in various genres of film, television, or new media scripts. Prerequisite: CTWR 514b.

WRIT 150.description: Writing and Critical Reasoning--Thematic Approaches. Academic writing, emphasizing analysis and argumentation, rhetorical judgment, critical reasoning, creative insight, the careful use of evidence, ethical perspectives, logical organization, stylistic and grammatical fluency. Duplicates credit in WRIT 130 and WRIT 140.

WRIT 320.description: Experiential Learning. A writing workshop that allows students to deepen their writing skills while working collaboratively with diverse groups, programs, or populations outside of USC.

WRIT 340.description: Advanced Writing and Critical Engagement. Advanced writing emphasizing critical engagement with disciplinary  practices and ethics, enabling students to produce effective  professional writing and participate responsibly in public  discourse.

WRIT 380.description: Writing in Global Contexts. Integrates global travel with experiential learning as a means of helping students to sharpen their writing and critical reasoning skills.

WRIT 440.description: Writing in Practical Contexts. Advanced training in analytical and argumentative writing for particular purposes in professional and practical contexts.
